articles.title: Welsh independence divides opinion among young people
articles.summary: A body has been set up to consider the case for Welsh independence as well as more devolved powers.
articles.body:
Cerys and Patrick have a lot in common. They're both young, Welsh, and very interested in politics.

The one thing they don't agree on is Wales' future within the United Kingdom.

A leading academic said the conversation around Welsh independence "has become normalised" amongst young people.

This week, the Plaid Cymru Welsh government set up a new body to consider the case for Welsh independence, as well as more devolution for Cardiff Bay.

For Patrick, he thinks his country is better off in the UK with more devolved powers, while Cerys believes an independent nation could offer more opportunities to people.

Nationalist party Plaid formed a government in Wales for the first after winning 46 seats during the May 2026 Senedd election .

While it hasn't called for a referendum on independence, the second line of its constitution says: "As the National Party of Wales, the party's aims shall be: to secure independence for Wales in Europe."

Pro-union party Reform UK is the second biggest in the Senedd after winning 34 seats in May's election.

Its Welsh leader Helen Jenner said voters "do not want to see Wales ripped out of the United Kingdom" and said the commission was "ridiculous".

A recent poll by Survation for the pro-independence group YesCymru suggested people under 35 in Wales were more in favour of independence than their older peers.

"People feel left behind, especially my age," said Patrick, a 20-year-old student from Newport.

He added that he could understand why people were "energised and enthusiastic" about independence because of issues such as "student loans, the cost of living, the geopolitical scene".

But he said: "As of right now, I just do not think there is a case for it."

However, Patrick, said he would support further devolved powers for Wales within the union.

He said that "practical elements" such as whether there would be a border between Wales and England remain unanswered questions for him.

For Cerys, learning to speak Welsh as an adult and broadening her understanding of history led to a "realisation" that Wales "in reality deserved a lot better than we had been given in the past and in the present".

"I think if we were independent, we could offer people more opportunity here," said the 35-year-old from Bridgend.

She added she'd like Wales to have further powers over policing and justice - a policy area currently controlled by Westminster.

"People seem to be kind of dangling the carrot of more devolution and never actually giving it to us," she said.

"More powers would be great but I will believe in those powers when I see them and until then, I think our best option is independence."

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has previously said he was open to the idea of giving the Welsh government control of policing in Wales.

A leading academic from Cardiff University said "it's staggeringly important" that "young people are a majority in favour of independence".

"They see nothing strange or impossible about Wales becoming independent in the future," said Prof Laura McAllister, from the Welsh Governance Centre.

She said that there was "great scepticism" around the topic when you look at the opinions of people aged over 65, adding there was a "real demographic schism".

"There's going to need to be something much closer to support at least half the population supporting independence before there is any chance of a referendum being won," McAllister believes.

She added nobody "can afford to be complacent about the future of the union" because "the concept of the United Kingdom has no God-given right to survive in its current form".

"What we've seen in politics in recent times is that the potential for change is intrinsic to everything that happened," she said.

In 2024, McAllister co-chaired a commission which concluded Wales leaving the United Kingdom is a "viable" option .

With polling suggesting between 20% to 30% of people in Wales would be in favour of independence , academics have compared the current situation to Scotland in the years leading up to the independence referendum in 2014 .

"In some ways the situation here looks similar to Scotland in 2007," said Dr Jac Larner, a pollster and political analyst from Cardiff University, reflecting on when the Scottish National Party [SNP] took power.

"You might think now we have a party like Plaid Cymru, there's this inevitable march to this endless 50-50 that you see in Scotland, right?

"What's different here [in Wales] is that we still have a lot more hostility to the idea of devolution.

"You have about a third who want to get rid of the devolution altogether, maybe just less than a third who want independence."

First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth said: "I have a vision for Wales, I support an independent Wales."

He said it was about "improving a lot of the people of Wales, tackling injustices, tackling unfairness, tackling inequalities, creating prosperity".

He added: "In the here and now, I deal with those issues dealing with the UK prime minister."

In October, the first ministers of Wales and Scotland met with Prime Minister Andy Burnham in Glasgow for the National Economic Council , where devolution and funding were discussed.

Ap Iorwerth said there was "a new understanding of the injustice of rail expenditure in Wales" from Burnham, as well as "a realisation that this hasn't been given enough attention politically by UK governments in the past".

Following the 2026 Autumn Budget , ap Iorwerth told BBC Wales there were " paltry sums of money coming on rail , when they've said there's £14bn on the way" and a "real terms cut in the money we have to spend on public services".

A UK government spokesman said: "The prime minister passionately believes in our union and is optimistic about the future of the United Kingdom.

"Our position on referendums is clear - the prime minister is focused on practical solutions to help people with the cost of living and make a positive difference in people's everyday lives, not constitutional questions.

"Through the convening power of No10 North , the prime minister will build a constructive working relationship with each devolved government to explore how we can together contribute to regional empowerment, reindustrialisation and achieving good growth in every postcode."

articles.title: Outlook fora do ar: Microsoft tem dificuldades para solucionar falha | G1
articles.standfirst: Ferramentas como o aplicativo de mensagens Teams, o Microsoft 365 (anteriormente Office) e o chatbot de inteligência artificial (IA) Copilot também foram atingidos por "problemas de conectividade".
articles.summary: Ferramentas como o aplicativo de mensagens Teams, o Microsoft 365 e o chatbot de inteligência artificial (IA) Copilot também foram atingidos por "problemas de conectividade"
articles.body:
Milhares de usuários da Microsoft continuam sem acesso a serviços como o e-mail Outlook na manhã desta sexta-feira (13). A Microsoft enfrenta dificuldades para solucionar uma grande falha global em seus serviços, iniciada ainda na tarde da quinta-feira (12).

Ferramentas como o aplicativo de mensagens Teams, o Microsoft 365 (anteriormente Office) e o chatbot de inteligência artificial (IA) Copilot também foram atingidos por "problemas de conectividade".

A Microsoft afirmou que a interrupção em seus serviços não foi provocada por um incidente de segurança cibernética, mas que os trabalhos para corrigir a falha têm sido infrutíferos.

Em uma atualização na manhã desta sexta, a Microsoft afirmou que está vendo "sucesso marginal" nas tentativas de solucionar o problema - mas que ainda não está claro o que provocou a falha.

Antes, a empresa havia afirmado que o problema era causado por uma "indisponibilidade inesperada" em um grande número de servidores da empresa - potentes computadores que processam tarefas como ferramentas de trabalho e outros aplicativos. Essa indisponibilidade teria, segundo a empresa, sobrecarregado os servidore restantes.

A Microsoft diz ainda que dará detalhes sobre a causa do problema assim que ele for resolvido. "Vamos continuar tratando o incidente com urgência e prioridade até uma resolução total", diz.

A BBC apurou que não há indícios de que a interrupção tenha sido causada por um ataque cibernético.

Para organizações internacionais, essas ferramentas são essencias para a comunicação e a colaboração com colegas ao redor do mundo.

"Agradecemos a paciência de nossos clientes enquanto trabalhamos para restabelecer os serviços o mais breve possível", disse a empresa em um comunicado.

Posteriormente, a empresa alertou que alguns serviços que haviam sido restabelecidos "podem voltar a ficar indisponíveis", acrescentando que clientes "em qualquer região" poderiam ser afetados.

Veja abaixo o que sabemos sobre a falha nos serviços da Microsoft:

O serviço de e-mail do Outlook foi o mais afetado pela falha da Microsoft — Foto: Getty Images via BBC

Um porta-voz da Microsoft disse à Reuters que os problemas se concentravam no Exchange Online, o serviço que gerencia as caixas de correio do Microsoft 365.

Entre os problemas, os usuários podem não conseguir visualizar determinados arquivos ou detalhes em seus aplicativos de calendário, informou a Microsoft. O Copilot (serviço de inteligência artificial da empresa) também pode apresentar falhas.

Alguns usuários conseguem usar o Teams normalmente, tanto para enviar mensagens quanto para organizar reuniões e consultar calendários.

O serviço do Teams e o pacote Microsoft 365 também foram afetados — Foto: Getty Images via BBC

O número exato de usuários afetados ainda não foi confirmado pela Microsoft.

Segundo o site de monitoramento de falhas na internet 140 mil relatos de problemas com o Outlook por volta das 15h (horário de Brasília) em 74 países na noite da quinta-feira (12).

O número caiu para cerca de 34.490 no fim da tarde, segundo dados do site citados pela Reuters. Às 19h47, o site registrava, ainda, cerca de 13.000 relatos sobre o Microsoft 365 e 763 sobre o Teams.

O número de usuários afetados pode chegar a milhões em escala global. De acordo com o site da própria Microsoft, mais de 430 milhões de pessoas usam os aplicativos do Microsoft 365.

Como o software da Microsoft é usado por empresas em todo o mundo, pode haver um efeito cascata em outros países.

Foram impactados ainda serviços de IA com conexões com produtos da Microsoft.

A OpenAI, responsável pelo ChatGPT, informou que estava investigando um problema com as integrações aos serviços da Microsoft, no qual novas conexões poderiam ser interrompidas, fazendo com que as ferramentas não funcionassem conforme o esperado.

Por sua vez, a Anthropic afirmou ter identificado um problema com um provedor de nível superior que afeta sua conexão com o Microsoft 365.

Agências e serviços governamentais, incluindo o governo de Singapura e a agência de espionagem da Austrália, disseram ter sido afetados.

No Reino Unido, diversos consultórios de clínicos gerais alertaram para possíveis problemas. Alguns deles instruíram pacientes a fazerem perguntas urgentes por telefone, no lugar de enviar e-mails ou preencher formulários online.

A Microsoft negou que a falha em seus serviços seja provocada por um ataque cibernético e atribuiu o problema à "sobrecarga elevada" em sua infraestrutura.

O termo faz referência a situações em que os serviços estão lidando com "um volume de estresse" muito maior do que o usual.

No caso da falha da Microsoft, um grande número de servidores ficou "indisponível inesperadamente", segundo a empresa, o que sobrecarregou os servidores restantes.

Na manhã desta sexta-feira, a Microsoft informou ter observado um "sucesso marginal" nos esforços para corrigir a falha global.

Em seu último comunicado até a atualização desta reportagem, a Microsoft afirmou que continua monitorando os esforços para resolver o problema em todas as regiões e avalia a situação dos servidores para determinar o que precisa ser feito.

Em um comunicado anterior, a empresa havia dito que as tentativas de correção "não estavam surtindo o efeito esperado".

Troy Hunt, especialista australiano em segurança cibernética, afirmou à BBC que a interrupção pode ter consequências de longo alcance.

"A Microsoft é parte essencial da infraestrutura da internet e nos faz lembrar da importância que o email ainda tem", afirma.

"Essa interrupção afeta não só a capacidade de muitas pessoas de trabalhar, mas também a capacidade de se comunicar sobre compromissos, comprar coisas que precisam de verificação, criar ou acessar contas e serviços", pontua.

Paul Spain, da empresa de consultoria Gorilla Technology, da Nova Zelândia, diz que, com e-mails e serviços offline, algumas empresas praticamente "perderam um dia útil".

articles.title: VÍDEO: Alpacas em casa de repouso na Alemanha alegram rotina de idosos | G1
articles.standfirst: Animais vivem em lar de repouso em Berlim há 12 anos. Residentes dizem que os bichos alegram o dia a dia.
articles.summary: No Mana Residence, em Berlim, alpacas em casa de repouso circulam livremente pelos quartos e jardins, promovendo bem-estar e confiança para os residentes idosos.
articles.body:
Em Berlim , na Alemanha, um lar de idosos possui residentes muito especiais. As alpacas fazem parte da Mana Residence há 12 anos e têm livre acesso a toda a propriedade e aos quartos dos residentes.

Para a diretora administrativa da casa, Johanna Janssen, os animais inspiram "pura alegria e confiança" nos moradores.

Max Beier, zelador e tratador de alpacas do Mana Residences, afirma que os animais são muito fáceis de cuidar e nunca são forçados a fazer nada.

"Quando entram na sala, ficam tão felizes", diz Beier. "E fazer alguém feliz é realmente a maior alegria que alguém pode ter." Além da felicidade que proporcionam às pessoas, elas também ajudam Beier em suas tarefas de jardinagem, mantendo a grama aparada.

Alpacas alegram o dia de idosos em casa de repouso em Berlim, Alemanha. — Foto: Reuters

Para Gerhard Guettler, morador local, as alpacas são mais do que apenas uma forma de diversão; elas o mantêm ativo.

"Eles ajudam e apoiam você durante todo o processo, e isso faz toda a diferença. É como se eles aparecessem e dissessem: 'Vamos lá, precisamos de algo de você'", diz Guettler, de 94 anos.

"E então, contanto que eu esteja me sentindo bem o suficiente, eu me levanto, vou até elas e nos divertimos um pouco juntos aqui" , afirma Guettler.

articles.title: Prédio desaba no Quênia e mata pelo menos seis pessoas | G1
articles.standfirst: Desabamentos no país são frequentes e causados ​​principalmente por mão de obra deficiente, materiais de qualidade inferior, supervisão inadequada e projetos estruturais falhos.
articles.summary: Prédio desaba no Quênia deixando seis mortos e três feridos; acidente evidencia falhas graves em construções que têm causado tragédias recorrentes no país.
articles.body:
Desabamento no Quênia deixa vítimas fatais em 13 de novembro de 2026. — Foto: Reuters

Pelo menos seis pessoas morreram nesta sexta-feira (13) depois de um prédio em construção desabar perto de Nairóbi, capital do Quênia.

De acordo com a imprensa local, o acidente ocorreu semanas depois de um outro edifício também ter desabado na capital queniana. Oito pessoas morreram no acidente.

Pelas redes sociais, a Cruz Vermelha do Quênia informou que pelo menos três pessoas foram resgatadas e levadas para o hospital.

Os desabamentos de edifícios no Quênia são frequentes e causados ​​principalmente por mão de obra deficiente, materiais de qualidade inferior, supervisão inadequada e projetos estruturais falhos, entre outros fatores, de acordo com o Instituto Queniano de Pesquisa e Análise de Políticas Públicas.

articles.title: Falha no Outlook, Teams e Copilot rende memes nas redes sociais | G1
articles.standfirst: Problemas em sistemas da Microsoft começaram na quinta-feira (12) e continuaram nesta sexta. Empresa informou que os serviços estão sendo restabelecidos gradualmente, mas usuários ainda podem enfrentar instabilidade.
articles.summary: Problemas em sistemas da Microsoft começaram na quinta-feira (12) e continuaram nesta sexta. Empresa informou que os serviços estão sendo restabelecidos gradualmente, mas usuários ainda podem enfrentar instabilidade.
articles.body:
A falha nos serviços da Microsoft virou tema de memes nas redes sociais nesta sexta-feira (13). Usuários têm relatado dificuldades para acessar o Outlook, o Teams e o assistente de inteligência artificial Copilot.

Segundo o Downdetector, plataforma que monitora falhas em serviços digitais, as reclamações começaram na tarde de quinta-feira (12) e continuaram durante a madrugada desta sexta-feira (13).

Atualização: A Microsoft informou na manhã da sexta-feira (13) que Outlook, Teams e Copilot estão sendo "gradualmente restaurados". Segundo a companhia, já houve melhorias em regiões da Europa e da América do Norte, mas alguns usuários ainda podem enfrentar problemas intermitentes durante a recuperação.

À medida que os sistemas da Microsoft foram retornando , os usuários voltaram a fazer memes, dessa vez, para comemorar (ou lamentar, não se sabe).

No meio da manhã desta sexta-feira, a Microsoft informou que Outlook, Teams e Copilot estão sendo "gradualmente restaurados" após a falha que afeta seus serviços desde a tarde de quinta-feira (12).

A empresa já descartou a hipótese de um ataque hacker. Segundo a companhia, já houve melhorias em regiões da Europa, da América do Norte e da Ásia, mas alguns usuários ainda podem enfrentar problemas intermitentes durante a recuperação.

articles.title: Taubaté tem 46 câmeras de comerciantes integradas ao sistema de monitoramento da Prefeitura; número está estagnado desde abril | G1
articles.standfirst: Adesão ao Programa Sentinela é voluntária e permite que imagens de estabelecimentos sejam acompanhadas pelo Centro de Gestão Integrada.
articles.summary: Adesão ao Programa Sentinela é voluntária e permite que imagens de estabelecimentos sejam acompanhadas pelo Centro de Gestão Integrada.
articles.body:
Imagem de arquivo - Câmeras de monitoramento em Taubaté — Foto: Reprodução/TV Vanguarda

O número de câmeras de segurança de comerciantes e moradores que compartilham imagens com a Prefeitura de Taubaté está parado desde abril. Atualmente, 46 equipamentos fazem parte do projeto Sentinela, que permite o acompanhamento das gravações pelo Centro de Gestão Integrada (CGI) do município. A participação é voluntária, mas a adesão ainda é baixa.

O programa começou a integrar câmeras particulares ao sistema municipal no ano passado . No CGI, agentes de segurança acompanham imagens de equipamentos instalados em vias públicas e de estabelecimentos que aderiram à iniciativa.

Segundo o comandante da Guarda Civil Municipal de Taubaté, Carlos Eduardo Santos, o compartilhamento pode contribuir tanto para a prevenção quanto para a investigação de crimes.

"A segurança é dever do Estado, do município, e logicamente a população pode participar, compartilhando essas imagens para que o poder público, juntamente com os órgãos de segurança, consigam dar continuidade à redução da criminalidade na cidade", afirmou.

De acordo com a Secretaria de Segurança Pública do Estado de São Paulo, os registros de furtos em Taubaté diminuíram na comparação entre janeiro e setembro de 2025 e o mesmo período de 2026. Foram 2.207 ocorrências no ano passado e 2.036 neste ano.

O comandante também afirmou que as imagens compartilhadas são armazenadas em um servidor da Prefeitura, com o objetivo de evitar vazamentos.

"As imagens são captadas, salvas no servidor diretamente do sistema para que não exista risco de vazamento de imagens que estão sendo compartilhadas para uso da prefeitura no processo de monitoramento da nossa cidade", explicou.

O especialista em segurança pública Frediano Teodoro ressalta, no entanto, que o monitoramento precisa seguir critérios para garantir a proteção dos dados e a privacidade de quem participa do projeto.

"Uma captação de imagens que, se não for bem tratada, protegida, pode chegar às mãos de pessoas que não deveriam ter acesso a esse tipo de material", alertou.

Moradores e comerciantes interessados em participar do Sentinela podem acessar o site da Prefeitura de Taubaté e buscar informações sobre o projeto.

articles.standfirst: Novas vagas devem atender demanda durante o período de fim de ano e funcionarão até o fim de janeiro de 2027.
articles.summary: Zona Azul em Taubaté ganha 100 novas vagas em ruas centrais para facilitar o acesso às lojas durante o fim de ano; medida vale até o dia 31 de janeiro.
articles.body:
Placa da zona azul em Taubaté — Foto: Reprodução/TV Vanguarda

A Prefeitura de Taubaté vai ampliar o número de vagas do serivço de Zona Azul na região central da cidade a partir de segunda-feira (16).

De acordo com as informações apuradas, serão criadas cerca de 100 novas vagas que vão ficar disponíveis até o dia 31 de janeiro, pensando no maior movimento durante o fim de ano.

As novas vagas estão previstas para três endereços: na Rua Coronel Marcondes de Mattos, na Rua Visconde do Rio Branco e na Rua Chiquinha de Mattos.

Segundo a Prefeitura, a medida vai ajudar o acesso dos consumidores às lojas da região central da cidade.

articles.title: Onça-parda e veado: monitoramento ajuda a preservar fauna no PI | G1
articles.standfirst: Imagens divulgadas na quinta-feira (12) mostram veados, pica-paus e outras espécies registradas por câmeras de monitoramento instaladas em Santa Rosa do Piau.
articles.summary: Imagens divulgadas na quinta-feira (12) mostram veados, pica-paus e outras espécies registradas por câmeras de monitoramento instaladas em Santa Rosa do Piau.
articles.body:
Imagens registradas por câmeras de monitoramento na localidade Morrinhos, em Santa Rosa do Piauí , no Sudeste do estado, ajudam a preservar a fauna silvestre da região. O equipamento flagrou diferentes espécies de animais, como veados, pica-paus, tucanos e gambás.

Entre os registros, o que mais chamou atenção foi o de uma onça-pintada. O acompanhamento dos animais é realizado pela Secretaria Municipal de Agricultura e Meio Ambiente de Santa Rosa do Piauí.

"Cada registro é importante para ampliar o conhecimento sobre as espécies que habitam nosso território e compreender a importância dos ambientes naturais para sua sobrevivência", afirmou a secretaria.

"A fauna silvestre desempenha um papel fundamental no equilíbrio dos ecossistemas, ajudando a manter a biodiversidade e os processos naturais da Caatinga", explicou a secretaria na postagem.

O diretor de Agricultura da pasta, Ricardo Missias, destacou que os registros reforçam a importância de preservar os ambientes naturais e a biodiversidade da região .

Ele explicou ainda que considera gratificante acompanhar as imagens e ver a presença dos animais na região. Segundo o diretor, a iniciativa de monitorar os animais surgiu da própria secretaria.

Imagens divulgadas na quinta-feira (12) mostram diferentes espécies de animais circulando nas proximidades das câmeras instaladas na localidade.

Segundo levantamento da secretaria, outras espécies também foram identificadas na área monitorada. Entre elas estão raposas, seriemas, gaviões, cancões, camundongos e tamanduás-mirins.

articles.title: US Navy quietly removes top commanders, draws congressional backlash
articles.summary: The US Navy has quietly removed or fired several senior officers and officials in recent months without its customary public announcements, drawing
articles.body: The US Navy has quietly removed or fired several senior officers and officials in recent months without its customary public announcements, drawing criticism from lawmakers over a lack of transparency and failure to inform Congress about key personnel changes.Two Democratic lawmakers on Thursday accused the Navy of withholding information about the removal of the entire leadership team of a nuclear-powered attack submarine following an underwater collision last month. Separately, the Navy also dismissed the commander of a destroyer deployed to the Middle East in September, while its attending physician for Congress and the Supreme Court departed amid an internal investigation.The developments mark a departure from the Navy's longstanding practice of publicly announcing the removal of senior commanders and other high-profile officials. They also come amid growing restrictions on the release of information about US military operations, particularly in the Middle East.In a letter to acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao and the service's top uniformed officer, Adm. Daryl Caudle, Democratic Reps. Joe Courtney of Connecticut and Adam Smith of Washington expressed concern over the Navy's failure to notify the House Armed Services Committee about the dismissal of the commander, second-in-command and top enlisted sailor of the USS South Dakota submarine.The lawmakers said the three officers were removed after the submarine struck an unidentified object on the seabed. However, the Navy declined to publicly comment on the incident or the subsequent personnel action.“As a result of the Navy’s failure to communicate, what should have been a standard exercise in information sharing has instead raised questions about the Navy’s commitment to transparency and its commitment to a productive working relationship with Congress,” the lawmakers wrote.The letter also expressed “deep frustration” over the Navy's failure to inform the committee about the submarine leadership changes.Destroyer commander removed amid Iran operationsIn a separate development, the Navy on September 27 relieved Cmdr. Caitlin Cunningham of her command of the USS Michael Murphy destroyer, which has been deployed to support operations against Iran, according to a defence official who spoke on condition of anonymity.Cunningham was removed due to a loss of confidence and had held the position for less than a year, the official said.The Navy did not publicly announce her removal, even when questioned about the personnel change. Such dismissals are typically disclosed within days, marking another departure from the service's usual communication practices.Navy physician departs amid investigationThe departure of Rear Adm. Dr Brian Monahan, who served as the attending physician for Congress and the Supreme Court, has also drawn attention.Republican Sen. Mike Rounds of South Dakota and Democratic Sen. Alex Padilla of California confirmed his departure on Thursday but provided few details about the circumstances.The Navy has opened an investigation into the matter, according to a person familiar with the situation who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to discuss it.Monahan served for nearly 18 years as the head of the Office of the Attending Physician, which provides emergency medical assistance to members of Congress and the Supreme Court, as well as congressional staff and visitors.He had previously attracted public attention for discussing the health of Senate Republican leader Mitch McConnell and administering a Covid-19 vaccine to then-House Speaker Nancy Pelosi.Growing restrictions on military informationThe developments come amid broader restrictions on the disclosure of information about US military activities, particularly in the Middle East.US Central Command, which oversees American military operations in the region, has released limited details about recent strikes on Iran. It has also declined to comment on the extent of damage to military bases and equipment, frequently citing operational security concerns.Access to satellite imagery has also faced restrictions. Major satellite imagery providers holding US government contracts have blocked or delayed the public release of images from the region at the request of American officials.These restrictions have made it difficult to assess the impact of Iranian attacks on US military installations. An Associated Press analysis found that it took months to establish that Iranian drone and missile strikes had damaged or destroyed structures at 26 military bases and other sites housing US equipment across the region.The Navy's handling of the recent personnel changes could also become an issue during next week's confirmation hearing for Hung Cao, who is seeking permanent appointment as the service's top civilian official.You use AI every day. articles.title: Australian billionaire Nicola Forrest donated around $500 million to her new foundation; the money will support Indigenous children and women entrepreneurs
articles.summary: Australian billionaire Nicola Forrest has donated more than $500 million to her Coaxial Foundation in 2026, with the funding supporting initiatives for
articles.body: Australian billionaire Nicola Forrest has donated more than $500 million to her Coaxial Foundation in 2026, with the funding supporting initiatives for Indigenous children and female entrepreneurs. The donation, comprising $125 million in cash and 25 million Fortescue shares, has enabled the foundation to announce its first three major long-term partnerships. These include up to $30 million for venture firm Antler to support up to 250 Australian female founders, $30 million over six years for Cape York Partnership to fund early learning initiatives for Aboriginal children, and $7.1 million over three years for SNAICC to improve early childhood learning outcomes for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children.Nicola Forrest’s foundation announces its first three major partnershipsCoaxial Foundation announced its first three major long-term partnerships as part of its commitment to expanding opportunities for women and children. The foundation said the partnerships were selected to support organisations with the expertise and experience needed to create lasting change.The announcement includes an up to $30 million partnership with Antler, a $30 million commitment to Cape York Partnership over six years, and a three-year partnership worth $7.1 million with SNAICC. These initiatives will provide funding, investment opportunities and programme support across entrepreneurship, early childhood learning and family development.Antler partnership will provide funding and business support to women foundersOne of the foundation's major commitments is an up to $30 million partnership with Antler, a global early-stage venture firm. The partnership will support up to 250 Australian female founders by providing access to funding, business networks and support during the early stages of building their companies.According to Coaxial Foundation, the partnership includes up to $10 million in non-dilutive funding, co-investments and programme support over four years. It also includes a $20 million investment into Antler Australia Fund III. The initiative aims to help female founders access the capital and resources required to develop their businesses.The partnership will also establish Momentum, powered by Coaxial, a dedicated four-year programme designed to identify, fund and support female founders. It will combine Antler's global venture platform with funding and investment support from Coaxial Foundation.Forrest’s foundation backs early childhood development in Cape YorkCoaxial Foundation has committed $30 million over six years to Cape York Partnership, an organisation working with Aboriginal communities. The funding will support learning and development initiatives for young Aboriginal children in the Cape.The partnership forms part of the foundation's broader commitment to improving opportunities for Indigenous children and families. Through the initiative, Cape York Partnership will receive long-term financial support for its work in early childhood learning and development.SNAICC partnership aims to strengthen early learning for Indigenous childrenThe foundation has also announced a three-year partnership worth $7.1 million with SNAICC – National Voice for our Children, the national peak body for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children and families.The funding will be provided through grants and philanthropic support to strengthen SNAICC's ability to support early childhood learning outcomes for Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children across Australia. The partnership will focus on helping the organisation extend its existing work with Indigenous families and communities.Coaxial CEO Philippa Watson said the foundation's partnerships with Cape York Partnership and SNAICC were long-term commitments to Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children and families. She said the initiatives would provide children with access to early learning opportunities that could be scaled to strengthen family systems and improve outcomes.Forrest outlines her vision for long-term philanthropic investmentNicola Forrest said the partnerships reflected her belief that philanthropy could act as an initial catalyst for change, while sustainable improvements required long-term investment and support.In the official media release, Ms Forrest said: "Australia does not have a shortage of talent, ambition or people committed to making things better. Too often, what is missing is access to opportunity, capital and the sustained support required to turn potential into outcomes."She also highlighted the importance of working with experienced organisations and maintaining long-term commitments. Reflecting on her experience in business and philanthropy, she said: "Thirty years in business and philanthropy have taught me that good intentions are not enough. Lasting change requires strong partners, evidence, disciplined execution and the willingness to stay the course."Coaxial Foundation said the three partnerships were among its first commitments following Forrest's initial donation of more than $500 million. The foundation described the announcement as the beginning of a broader programme of long-term investment in initiatives intended to create meaningful impact.You use AI every day. articles.title: Outlander star Sam Heughan went back to the Scottish drama school where he trained to fund three scholarships every year; his separate creative award selected new student winners again in 2026, including a £2,500 grant
articles.summary: Actor Sam Heughan is using the success he found through acting to help the next generation of performers get their start.
articles.body: Actor Sam Heughan is using the success he found through acting to help the next generation of performers get their start. The Outlander star, who trained at the Royal Conservatoire of Scotland (RCS) in Glasgow, has committed to funding three annual scholarships for students pursuing undergraduate studies at the institution. He has also created a separate initiative that gives emerging artists financial support to develop their own creative projects. According to the Royal Conservatoire of Scotland and its May 2026 announcement, Heughan's contribution extends beyond tuition assistance. Through his scholarship programme and the Write Start creative commission, he is helping students gain access to opportunities, mentorship and resources that can make it easier to take their first steps into the performing arts industry.From student to supporterHeughan's connection with the institution is a personal one. Born in Balmaclellan, Dumfries and Galloway, the actor graduated from RCS with a BA in Acting in 2003. He went on to build an international career, becoming widely recognised for playing Jamie Fraser in the historical fantasy series Outlander, based on Diana Gabaldon's novels.In July 2021, he announced his ten-year scholarship commitment, returning to the institution to help students who might otherwise struggle to afford studying in Glasgow. The programme provides three scholarships each academic year. Two are intended for Scottish students entering the BA Acting course, while the third supports a student from outside Scotland studying within the School of Stage and Screen. The financial assistance is intended to make professional arts education more accessible, particularly for students who face financial barriers to pursuing their ambitions. His contribution was also recognised by the conservatoire in 2022, when he received an honorary doctorate and returned to attend its graduation ceremony.A separate platform for student creativityAlongside the scholarships, Heughan established Write Start: The Sam Heughan Creative Commission in 2021. Unlike the scholarship programme, which helps students with their education, this annual initiative focuses on helping them turn original ideas into finished creative projects.The competition encourages collaboration between students from different disciplines, including music, acting, dance, filmmaking and production. It provides funding and professional guidance, giving students the opportunity to experiment with ideas that might otherwise remain on paper. The 2026 edition recognised projects that brought together different artistic approaches, with two main winners receiving £2,500 each and runners-up receiving £500.Meet the 2026 winnersAmong this year's recipients was music student Bohdan Ilnytskyi, who won the School of Music category for his project Some of Us. The £2,500 grant will support his exploration of how music can drive storytelling in films, rather than simply accompany scenes. His work also looks at incorporating Ukrainian musical instruments, including the kobza, into contemporary screen compositions. The School of Music runner-up award went to Isla Hallewell and her six-member ensemble, Mother Tongues: Ancient Folk. Their project will explore the relationship between historical Baroque music and folk traditions through a collaborative programme involving the University of Oxford and the Bates Instrument Collection.In the School of Stage and Screen category, second-year acting student Robert (Robbie) Greenhalgh received the other £2,500 award. His project, Swim Until You Can't See Land, will be developed with fellow students Shay McFadden and Morven Blackadder. The proposed theatre production or feature film draws inspiration from Scottish band Frightened Rabbit and its late frontman Scott Hutchison.The story follows a young man returning to his seaside hometown on Scotland's east coast after his brother's death, exploring grief, identity and the complicated relationship people have with the places they come from. The £500 runner-up award in the same category went to acting students Wren Callender, Kit Allen and Marcela Weltsek-Medina. Their project, The Boy and the Rat Bastard, is a queer satirical animated television concept for which they plan to develop a teaser trailer. The next edition of Write Start is expected to open for applications in 2027, with details due towards the end of the year.Through these two initiatives, Heughan has created different avenues for students to pursue their ambitions, whether by making formal training more affordable or giving original ideas the financial backing needed to take shape. For someone who once walked the same corridors as these aspiring performers, the effort is also a way of helping ensure that financial circumstances do not determine who gets the opportunity to build a career in the arts.You use AI every day. articles.title: Chelmsford boy died from multiple injuries in Cyprus hotel fall
articles.summary: An Essex coroner describes Jaxon Foster's death as "particularly tragic" as he opens an inquest.
articles.body:
A two-year-old boy who fell to his death from a fourth-floor window of a Cyprus hotel died from multiple severe injuries, a coroner has said.

Jaxon Foster tumbled nearly 40ft (12m) at the five-star King Evelthon Beach Hotel and Resort on 12 July, the first day of his family holiday in Chlorakas.

The boy, from Chelmsford, suffered fatal injuries to his head, vital organs and body, an inquest at Essex Coroner's Court has heard. The inquest was opened and adjourned on Friday.

Jaxon's father, Joshua, was fined €3,000 (£2,500) at a court in Paphos in October, having admitted causing his death through a reckless, rash or dangerous act.

Foster's sentencing hearing was told he had placed Jaxon on a windowsill to show him the view of a waterpark, but had failed to realise the window was open.

The 37-year-old auditor's lawyer branded it "a momentary error" with "fatal consequences".

On Friday, Lincoln Brookes, Essex's senior coroner, said it was a "particularly tragic" case.

"This two-year-old child was on holiday with his family in Paphos in Cyprus," Brookes said.

"He sadly fell from a window on the fourth floor of the hotel the family were staying at and, sadly, his death was confirmed that same day at the hospital."

Jaxon's provisional cause of death was given as "severe craniocerebral injuries and multiple injuries of the body and vital organs" due to a fall from height.

The coroner said a full inquest would be heard on 6 January, and offered his condolences to Jaxon's family.

In a statement, the family previously said: "Our son was deeply loved and will be forever missed. His loss is something we carry with us every day."

Foster arrived in Cyprus with his wife, two children and in-laws hours before the incident.

They enjoyed time by the swimming pool before getting ready for dinner in the evening.

Foster, his father-in-law and Jaxon were walking towards a lift at about 18:00 when the boy noticed a waterpark outside, his sentencing hearing was told.

Foster pushed the lift button, placed Jaxon on the windowsill and then could not react before his son fell.

District Judge Froso Christodoulidou said in October: "The window did not appear to carry markings that would necessarily have alerted the defendant to the fact that one section was open."

She added there was no evidence Foster "deliberately exposed the child to danger" and that no sentence could outweigh the consequences of losing Jaxon.

Foster's lawyer, Alexandros Alexandrou, described him as an "incredible father" with a "beautiful family".

articles.title: A million mood boards later, there’s still only one Sade
articles.summary: The Rock & Roll Hall of Fame inductee’s style, like all great art, appears easy to pull off — yet is anything but.
articles.body: Despite being one of the world’s most elusive artists, Sade Adu remains instantly recognizable. Whether it be her sultry whisper of a voice drifting through a vast catalogue of hits on the radio (and, these days, TikTok), or her signature sleek style inspiring countless digital mood boards, the British-Nigerian musician’s artistry has long been revered. Now, with over 50 million albums sold, the singer and her band –– both known simply by her first name –– will be inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame this weekend. It’s a fitting time to reflect on her highly revered style, which like all great art appears easy to pull off –– yet is anything but. Having graduated with a degree in fashion design from London’s Central Saint Martins in 1979, Sade understood the art of a garment better than most of her 1980s pop peers. With a background in menswear design, her acute attention to silhouette and form shaped her sartorial point of view. Unlike today’s A-listers, Sade doesn’t rely on a stylist for her performances or (extremely rare) public appearances. (Days before Saturday’s official Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction ceremony, Sade and her band announced that they would not appear in person to accept the honor, a move that speaks volumes of a lifelong dedication to her privacy.) Since her debut alongside bandmates in 1982, Sade applied her design training to whatever she wore on and off the stage. Backless bodysuits with pristinely tailored trousers. Crisp button downs tied at the belly button and cropped bolero jackets. Her gold, oversized hoop earrings and a satin red lipstick were practically non-negotiable. The star has become something of a deified godmother of minimalist fashion over the decades. But reducing her approach to “quiet luxury” or “clean girl” dressing feels, if anything, insulting to the authenticity and intentionality behind her looks. Sade was very much a lover of style, while rejecting the at times rampant frivolousness of fashion. “I don’t really like the fashion industry, to be honest with you. I don’t like the way it works, the way buyers have so much power over everything — who’s their darling this week and so forth,” Sade told Interview magazine for her 1988 cover story. “I think it’s far more cutthroat than the music business. I find it a bit distasteful and have never really been part of that… I don’t like fashion, but I do like clothes.” Despite her reluctance to embrace the fashion world, Sade’s influence has still managed to transcend. “It was interesting to see a Black woman at that time who was so pared back. This was in the era of Whitney Houston, Janet Jackson, Madonna — a lot of glam and a lot of hair,” said Emil Wilbekin, a professor at New York’s Fashion Institute of Technology and a former editor in chief of Vibe magazine. “Here’s this woman who was just super- duper clean beauty before clean beauty was a thing, but it was also her actual style. It’s like a t-shirt, jeans, a flat and a bolero jacket and let’s go.” Music journalist and author Clover Hope describes Sade’s presence as “accessible and aspirational at the same time.” “My earliest memories are looks from her music videos. For ‘Smooth Operator,’ she wore that open-backed, boat-neck white dress with a braided ponytail. She’s kind of barely in the video, but I remember watching it as a teenager and thinking she looked like Josephine Baker or an old Hollywood star,” Hope continued. “Or the video for ‘Never As Good As the First Time,’ where she’s riding a horse in a white button-up that’s tied in the front. She had a kind of sexy, cool presence about her that played a big role in her being able to pull off these looks.” The singer has always been able to effortlessly sync on-stage glamour with the easygoing everyday attitude of streetwear — before we even used the term. She could mesmerize a crowd just as easily in a crystal embellished skirt set, as she could clad in a knit sweater and loafers. “I think because she studied fashion and menswear she really understood using fashion as a tool to blend this masculine femininity,” said fashion journalist Shelton Boyd Griffith. “One of my favorite videos from Sade is ‘Turn My Back On You’ where she and her bandmates are all dressed up in suits with ties but then she has the red lip and the hoops and the hair. You have this very muggy, femme face but then dressed in this edgy suit. She’s very comparable to Grace Jones. They both pioneered mixing womenswear and menswear during that time.” Wilbekin agrees that Sade’s subtle gender-bending still carries heavy influence today. “She really kind of was ahead of her time in terms of the sartorial idea of incorporating male tailoring and dressing and androgyny, but with very simplistic beauty, which is how everyone dresses now,” Wilbekin added. While several Black artists from decades past who have contributed to pop culture at large are often overlooked, the Sade effect has been the opposite. Without trying, her style and sound has only continued to garner mass appeal, gaining another life through our social algorithms and places like Pinterest. In the last twelve months alone, Sade-specific terms have seen year-over-year growth on Pinterest like “Sade Outfits,” (+77%) “Sade Adu Hairstyle”(+29%), along with “Sade Makeup” (+15%) and “Slicked Back Hair Reference,”(+217%) according to the visual discovery platform. While at first glance Sade’s style seems easy enough to replicate, her magic doesn’t solely stem from the clothes she wears, as much as the overall aura she exudes. “She has never done too much. It’s always so breezy — like singing barefoot with a diamond skirt and your hair just flowing. That’s ‘it girl’ energy,” continued Boyd Griffith. “At the core of it all is uniform dressing that we’ve seen all over – we’ve seen it at Celine, we’ve seen it at Kallmeyer. Her denim Canadian tuxedo or her plain white tee and red lip are something that on the surface seems easy to replicate. I think Gen Z see her and think I could do that, too.” Hope reiterates that there are core elements that encapsulate the Sade look. “There is a Sade uniform, so to speak, although it wasn’t always exactly the same. It was more a concept,” she explained. “Her outfits leaned modest, but there was usually at least one bold element, whether it was a pop of color, a decorative detail, or an unexpected accessory like leather gloves. Sometimes a dress with a classic silhouette. They were outfits that didn’t look cumbersome on stage. Just stylish and practical.” Even though the band’s last full-length album was released 16 years ago, musically Sade continues to inspire everyone from fellow R&B songstresses Snoh Aalegra and SZA, to stars like Drake and Beyoncé. (Beyoncé even named Sade in 2021 as one of the reasons she has chosen to speak less to the press in recent years.) Her style legacy and her inherent sense of self lives on in modern day fashion favorites like Tracee Ellis Ross and Solange. “Because she’s been so in charge of her own career that magic just organically happens. One moment she could be a mermaid, and in the next video she’s dressed in light men’s drag,” said Boyd Griffith. “She effortlessly comes across because she’s so her, and very few artists are bold enough to just be themselves. She’s always been a woman who truly just knows herself.” Even while shunning the press limelight, there’s so much that Sade can continue to teach us about style. “We don’t have a lot of interviews of her. She really just exists within images now — but I think that was also intentional,” he added. “She wants the music to speak for itself.”

articles.title: Advice to patients in the West as Microsoft Outlook outage disrupts emails
articles.summary: Hospital trusts in Bristol, Gloucestershire, Somerset and Wiltshire are issuing guidance to patients.
articles.body:
Disruption to hospitals in the West of England is easing following a global Microsoft Outlook email outage .

Services including Teams, Outlook and AI software Copilot were impacted across the world, with Microsoft saying the cause was down to a "technical issue not related to cyber or AI/agents" . It apologised for the disruption.

By 14:00 GMT, the company said it was seeing improvements, "with email queues significantly reduced and approaching normal levels".

Bristol NHS Foundation Trust reassured patients earlier that essential hospital services and procedures were continuing as normal and has now said that fixes have been put in place, allowing services to properly resume.

The trust also said "some emails may still be delayed while systems recover" and asked patients to call the relevant number on their appointment letter if they have urgent questions.

Gloucestershire NHS Foundation Trust also said normal service had resumed but there could be some delays as systems catch up.

Bath and North East Somerset, Swindon and Wiltshire (BSW) Community Health said its services were also continuing to operate under "tried and tested business continuity plans" earlier in the day.

"Please continue to use our services and attend appointments as planned unless we contact you otherwise.

"We are experiencing increased demand on our phone lines, and thank you for your patience and understanding," it added.

Somerset NHS Foundation Trust said it was unaffected by the outage and all of its services were running as normal, although there could be some delays to sending and receiving e-mails.

A spokesperson for NHS Dorset, NHS Somerset and NHS Bath and North East Somerset, Swindon and Wiltshire ICBS cluster said they were experiencing some disruption to email services and local NHS services were enacting long-standing contingency plans to manage the situation.

NHS England said patients should continue to use 999 in an emergency, call 111, or attend their local pharmacy.

At about 09:30, Microsoft said it was seeing "early signs of stabilisation" but service capacity had "not yet returned to normal levels".

In its latest update at about 14:00, Microsoft said some users "may still experience intermittent access issues or delayed email delivery as recovery continues".

It added that it was "restoring the remaining affected infrastructure while investigating residual service issues" to ensure sustained service stability.

The global outage started on Thursday, with monitoring website Downdetector seeing problems reported in more than 70 countries.

Microsoft executive Charles Lamanna said the issue was not caused by a cyber-security incident, ruling out any malicious or hacking activity.

articles.title: MICHAEL RUIZ: JonBenet Ramsey investigators are retesting evidence with newer technology, police chief says
articles.summary: Boulder investigators are retesting decades-old DNA evidence in the JonBenet Ramsey cold case using advanced technology that didn't exist in 1997.
articles.body: Investigators in Boulder are retesting decades-old evidence in the murder of JonBenet Ramsey as her family nears 30 years since the unsolved slaying in their former Colorado home. "Chief [Steve] Redfearn and I are more hopeful now than we have been in the past because of the advances in the investigation and the advances in technology," Boulder County District Attorney Michael Dougherty told reporters in a news briefing this week. "And I say that based on just how DNA has progressed over time." Her father, John Ramsey, had spent years begging authorities to attempt to solve the case through investigative genetic genealogy, a relatively new technique for ginning up DNA leads that involves combining genetic testing results with genealogy research to identify potential persons of interest. IGG itself is rapidly evolving as state-of-the-art DNA testing also improves. And her brother, John Andrew Ramsey, told Fox News Digital he believes the samples in police possession do contain the DNA of JonBenet's killer. JONBENET RAMSEY'S FATHER ASKS TRUMP FOR HELP IN DAUGHTER'S UNSOLVED MURDER CASE "The testing available in the late 1990s was far less sensitive than today’s, yet it still detected this male DNA in the same spot as her blood," he said. "In 2008, touch DNA testing found the same unknown male’s DNA on both the left and right sides of the waistband of her long johns. It is the killer’s DNA." A cold case review panel was convened in Boulder as local police, state and federal investigators continue to dig into what happened on Dec. 26, 1996, when JonBenet was found strangled and with head trauma in the basement of her home. Although investigators have pursued a number of potential suspects, persons of interest and theories about how she died over the years, no one has been convicted, and her death remains one of America's most prominent unsolved cases. "It's no secret," Boulder Police Chief Steve Redfearn told reporters in a sit-down interview earlier this week. "We're also going back, based on that cold case review, and retesting things that were tested 30 years ago with newer technology." MICHAEL RUIZ: JONBENÉT RAMSEY'S FATHER CHALLENGES DA AFTER REPORT SAYS FAMILY SHOULDN'T HAVE BEEN CLEARED Redfearn appeared to confirm a recent revelation John Andrew Ramsey, who told Fox News Digital previously that the family had learned this year that new testing had begun in the fall of 2025. "Maybe something comes of that," Redfearn said. "Not that it was missed, but maybe the technology just improved enough that we look at, hey, this item was tested in '97, we're testing it again, and hey, look, we found something that was missed in '97." Dougherty gave an example of a recent trial that he said involved the testimony of four different DNA experts because testing had been done on multiple occasions as the technology improved. Among the benefits of rapidly improving technology is an increasingly successful ability to identify DNA profiles contained in mixed samples, Dougherty added. articles.title: Rosalía scoops historic third best album award at Latin Grammys
articles.summary: The Spanish singer is recognised for her fourth album Lux which was released last year to rave reviews.
articles.body:
Spanish star Rosalía has made history as the first woman to win the best album award at the Latin Grammys three times, after being recognised for her project Lux.

The singer took home five trophies in total, including two for her track La Perla which was named song of the year and best pop song.

La Perla was also nominated for record of the year but missed out to Argentine singer Milo J's song Niño.

Rosalía released Lux last year to rave reviews and collecting her award at the ceremony in Las Vegas on Thursday, she said: "To all the people who told me I wasn't good enough, or that my music was too weird, I'm thankful I didn't listen."

The Barcelona-born artist then added: "Now I'm winning these prizes."

Rosalía, who opened the ceremony with a performance of some of her biggest songs, was honoured with the prize for best alternative music album.

She also picked up best shortform music video for her track Sauvignon Blanc.

The singer had previously won best album for El Mal Querer in 2019 and Motomami in 2022 - and her third Lux is also tipped to be a favourite when nominations are announced for the Grammys next week.

It was also a big night for Puerto Rican reggaeton legend Daddy Yankee, who won the person of the year award.

He performed some of his best-loved tracks including Gasolina and Con Calma, and was joined on stage by rappers including LL Cool J and French Montana.

Punjabi singer Diljit Dosanjh, who collabed with Daddy Yankee on Pokito, even took a break from his Aura India tour for the set, making him the first Indian artist to perform at the Latin Grammys.

Dosanjh superfan Devanshi Arora described the singer's appearance as "a cultural revolution".

"It's really invigorating and motivating to see someone from my country has made it all around the world," she tells Newsbeat.

She sees a lot of similarities between South American and Punjabi communities and hopes this leads to more collaborations - with a link-up between Dosanjh and Bad Bunny top of her wishlist.

Daddy Yankee was presented with the lifetime achievement award by Janet Jackson, who told him in Spanish that his music "has inspired an entire generation".

Accepting the prize for record of the year, Milo J seemed surprised to have won ahead of strong competition from Karol G, Jorge Drexler, Carin León as well as Rosalía.

The 20-year-old took home four trophies in the end and gave a shout out to Argentine folk music.

He described Niño as the song "I'm most proud of out of everything I've created so far".

"Long live Argentine folk music," he added.

Elsewhere, ARIA VEGA was named best new artist and songwriter of the year went to Sara Schell.

articles.title: UN watchdog calls on Iran to reopen nuclear facilities to inspection
articles.summary: IAEA says it cannot verify whether an underground Iranian enrichment plant contains nuclear material.
articles.body:
The United Nations nuclear watchdog has urged Iran to allow it to resume inspections of its nuclear facilities.

The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) called for Tehran to restore access for its inspectors in a report circulated by the watchdog among member states on Friday, insisting the move is essential to carry out its remit to monitor the Iranian nuclear programme.

Iran has allowed only very limited IAEA inspections since the United States and Israel launched attacks on the country’s nuclear facilities in June 2025. The report said Tehran had told the organisation that it was not possible to allow the inspections to continue amid the current security situation.

The IAEA said the lack of information about Iran’s atomic sites and nuclear material is “a matter of proliferation concern” that “needs to be rectified with the utmost urgency,” The Associated Press news agency reported.

The watchdog noted that it is “fully prepared to resume its safeguards activities in Iran at short notice”.

The report expressed particular concern about an underground uranium-enrichment plant near Isfahan in central Iran, according to the Reuters news agency.

Tehran declared the Isfahan Fuel Enrichment Plant in 2025 but has not permitted the IAEA access to inspect the facility.

Inspectors still do not know the plant’s precise location, whether it holds nuclear material, or its status under international monitoring rules. The report did not establish that uranium enrichment is taking place there.

IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi urged Iran to consider limited technical measures that could make inspection visits possible and help restore routine monitoring, the AFP news agency said.

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said at a news conference in Tehran on Monday that Iran remained committed to the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty, which seeks to prevent the spread of nuclear weapons.

But he blamed US and Israeli attacks for limiting cooperation with the IAEA. Since the bombing of the nuclear facilities last year, the watchdog has been unable to verify the status of Iran’s stockpile of near-weapons-grade uranium, the report noted.

The IAEA withdrew its inspectors for safety reasons, and Iran later passed a law suspending cooperation with it.

The IAEA’s inspections are intended to verify that nuclear material is not diverted towards weapons. Without direct access to sites such as Isfahan, the agency cannot independently establish what is happening at those facilities.

However, the report notes that Iran told the IAEA this month that discussion on resuming inspections in the country cannot resume amid “persistent, explicit, and public threats by the President of the United States of America … to commit further acts of armed aggression”.

Iran said that the issue would not be resolved “until the root causes of the present situation are addressed and the essential requirements for normal safeguards implementation are restored,” the report added.

articles.title: Jersey Museum 'over the moon' at winning national award
articles.summary: It is the second year running the museum has won a Gold accolade at the VisitEngland awards.
articles.body:
Museum bosses are "over the moon" after winning a top national award for the second year running.

Jersey Museum was one of only 21 attractions that won a Gold accolade at the VisitEngland Visitor Attraction Accolades.

Louise Downie, Jersey Heritage's director of curation and experience, said: "We are over the moon about winning gold again for Jersey Museum."

She said the award, alongside positive feedback from visitors, confirmed improvements at the museum were benefiting people discovering Jersey's history and she highlighted the flagship exhibition La Tèrr'rie d'Jèrri and the new interactive exhibition Playing with Light.

Hamptonne Country Life Museum also received a Welcome Accolade for making visitors feel valued.

All six Jersey Heritage visitor sites received high assessment scores and attained VisitEngland's Quality Rose Marque following inspections earlier this year. The other sites are the Maritime Museum, La Hougue Bie, Mont Orgueil and Elizabeth Castle.

"Our staff work hard across all our sites to maintain high standards and to provide a wonderful experience for our visitors," said Downie.

"We are delighted for the team at Hamptonne for their well-earned Welcome award as well."

Although VisitEngland provides assessments for tourism and hospitality businesses in England, Jersey Heritage has taken part in the quality assessment scheme for a number of years and is assessed against the same standards.

The awards were presented at the British Motor Museum in Warwickshire.

articles.title: Pakistan military reports it killed 74 ‘terrorists’ during raids
articles.summary: Increased attacks on the border with Afghanistan have caused tensions between the neighbours.
articles.body:
Pakistan’s army has reported that it has killed 74 armed fighters in multiple raids in areas along the country’s borders with Afghanistan.

Thirty-one “terrorists” have been killed in the southwestern Balochistan province since November 3, with multiple weapons, explosives and ammunition recovered, the military’s news division said in a statement posted on social media on Friday.

Balochistan is the site of an armed rebellion waged by the Balochistan Liberation Army (BLA), which seeks independence from Pakistan for the region.

Another 35 fighters were killed in the past two days during separate raids on Mir Ali, while eight were killed in Orakzai, and weapons were recovered, the force added in an update.

Both districts are in the northern Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, where the Pakistan Taliban, known as the TTP, and several other armed groups are based.

Islamabad accuses India and Afghanistan of backing the armed groups, although Delhi and Kabul deny involvement.

“The security forces’ continued successes in the war against terrorism reflect national resolve and professional capabilities,” President Asif Ali Zardari said in a statement. “Operations must continue against externally sponsored terrorist elements seeking to undermine Pakistan’s security.”

The army identified the fighters as “Khawarij”, a term it uses to refer to fighters it says are backed by Afghanistan, including the TTP.

Although separate, the TTP is allied with the Afghan Taliban, which took power in 2021.

Pakistani authorities believe the group operates from areas on Afghanistan’s side of the border and is responsible for increased attacks on Pakistani territory in recent years.

The issue has strained relations between Islamabad and Kabul and led to armed confrontations resulting in civilian deaths.

At least 11 policemen were killed, and another 12 were wounded after alleged TTP fighters ambushed a convoy in the Kohat district of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa on Thursday, authorities said.

articles.title: The Italian waiter held our baby. Then the unexpected happened
articles.summary: First trip after cancer treatment, peed-on waiter, stolen car, tacos in taxis and a kid-sized faux pas. Welcome to the first round of CNN Travel’s short stories.
articles.body: Welcome to our first roundup of CNN Postcards: short first-person travel tales capturing the highs, and sometimes lows, of travel. We are kicking off this new series with contributions from CNN Travel staff, but we want to hear your stories and see your photos and video for possible inclusion in the series. A submission form awaits below the stories, which will hopefully inspire you to share! We gave the waiter a big tip It was a chilly April, but in the midday sun it was warm enough to sit on the balcony to eat prosciutto, local arugula and the exquisite jars of homemade tomato sauce sold by the woman down on the corner. Visiting out of season, we could afford to rent the clifftop house in Peschici and drink in endless views of the cold sea. Only one restaurant was open in the evening and we had the waiter to ourselves. He held our little girl so we could enjoy our meal, and laughed with genuine delight when she peed on him. (Barry Neild) The trip I willingly quarantined for Several months after I finished cancer treatment, still mid-pandemic, Sri Lanka reopened to travel. Without consulting my doctor, I booked a five-week itinerary around the island, figuring that was enough to make the quarantine awaiting me back in Hong Kong worth it. It was a series of incredible firsts: first visit to South Asia, first trip since getting sick, first time seeing elephants. At many of the country’s most popular attractions, there were very few tourists. Even though I have a mask on in this photo at the Dambulla Caves, I know there’s a giant smile behind it. (Lilit Marcus) For sale: Stolen car, good price A tangle of exposed wires spilled from the steering wheel. My girlfriend, Kate, noticed too, but we didn’t say anything to the nice man driving us to the outskirts of London, beyond the Tube, in what looked like a hot-wired vehicle. He was taking us to see another. Two Americans traveling abroad, we had the novel idea of buying a used car to drive around Europe. This was the most run-down one we’d seen. The radio was broken, the upholstery torn. After we politely said we weren’t interested, he suddenly drove off. We laughed. “Now how do we get back?” (David G. Allan) Hailing a taxi and maybe a taco Visiting Mexico with our toddler, we took taxis around Isla Mujeres, an island off Cancun. Hailing a cab one evening, we found other passengers already aboard. But they said nothing, so we squeezed in, my son balanced on my lap. We got used to sharing taxis. Then one day, a driver was accompanied by his family. With a stack of tortillas on the dashboard, his wife prepared beef tacos. She handed her husband a taco, then assembled one for her son. I can still see the boy’s big, sleepy eyes, and the taco made on the dashboard of his father’s taxi. (Jeanne Bonner) My first faux-pas They flitted onto the jungle gym beside me — first one child, then two. We hung silently, like crows gathered in “The Birds.” I’d faced challenges on this, my first French camping trip, but handled them with the full courage of my seven years. An explorer in a strange land, I’d hammered tent pegs and said “merci” to the ice-cream man. Alien sounds shot out of the boy’s mouth. The little girl stared, waiting for my response. I leapt off and ran back to the safety of my family. My cheeks flared hot with deep, enduring shame. I wasn’t cosmopolitan yet. (Maureen O’Hare) Submit your own postcard Do you have a brief story that could have only happened far from home? Did you fall in love with a place that you visited? Have you experienced a moment of immersion or an uncanny encounter while traveling? Submit your postcard below.

articles.title: Why is Ukraine attacking Russian warships in the Baltic Sea amid talks?
articles.summary: Finland says Ukraine struck a Russian warship near its coast as Kyiv and Moscow held US-brokered talks in Abu Dhabi.
articles.body:
Finland’s military says it detected “a strike” on a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland on Wednesday, as Ukraine sent waves of drones towards Russia’s northwestern Leningrad region.

The strike came as Russian and Ukrainian delegations met in Abu Dhabi for their first United States-brokered talks since February.

It was a rare strike on a Russian navy vessel in the Baltic Sea .

So why is Ukraine taking the war to the Baltic, and why now? Here’s what we know:

“The Finnish Defence Forces detected… a strike on a Russian warship in the Gulf of Finland area and has monitored the development of the situation,” a military spokesperson told the Reuters news agency in an emailed statement.

The spokesperson said Finland was not under any immediate military threat, but declined to say where or when the incident happened, or how it had been detected.

It was not immediately clear whether there were any casualties. Estonian media reported that the vessel was a small Russian navy ship that later returned to St Petersburg.

On Wednesday, drones also caused a fire in the Russian port area of Ust-Luga, injuring three workers, regional Governor Aleksandr Drozdenko said.

Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania told citizens to take shelter as drones strayed into their airspace, and NATO scrambled warplanes in response.

The Gulf of Finland is a narrow arm of the Baltic Sea between Finland and Estonia, both NATO members, that extends east to St Petersburg. Ust-Luga, on its southern shore, is a key export outlet for Russian oil and grain.

Several Ukrainian drones deployed towards the Leningrad region have strayed into the airspace of Finland and the Baltic states, raising fears that the war is spilling over into NATO countries that border Russia.

Finland’s Defence Minister Antti Hakkanen said Helsinki had raised the strike with Kyiv.

“We have told the Ukrainians this time, and a little earlier too, how sensitive this narrow stretch of the Gulf of Finland, right between us and Estonia, is in terms of environmental safety and the safety of civilian shipping,” he said, according to Finnish broadcaster Yle.

But he said the spillover effects in the surrounding region stem from Ukraine’s defensive fight and assured the public the Baltic Sea around Finland was still safe.

“You can still cruise with peace of mind,” he said.

Ilya Timtchenko, a fellow with the Transatlantic Defense and Security Program at the Center for European Policy Analysis, told Al Jazeera the strike was thought to be the first by Ukrainian forces on a Russian ship in an area of the Baltic used by civilian traffic.

“Ukraine and its European allies are showing that they are unified in their approach to fighting off the Russian threat,” he told Al Jazeera.

Ukraine’s Security Service said it attacked the Buyan-M-class small missile ship, Naro-Fominsk, as part of a special operation, according to Yle.

Meanwhile, Ukraine’s General Staff said the strike on Ust-Luga had damaged five fuel tanks.

“According to preliminary information, as a result of drone strikes on the port’s oil infrastructure, the tank network suffered the most damage,” it reported on Telegram.

On Thursday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Ireland and praised their mediation efforts.

Russia, Ukraine and the US held two days of talks in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and Wednesday. The last such talks took place in February this year.

The talks produced no breakthrough, apart from an agreement to swap a large number of prisoners. Russia’s state-run TASS news agency said the exchange should happen in two to three weeks.

Territory remains the main sticking point.

Ukraine wants Russia pushed back to the original border between the two countries, while Russian President Vladimir Putin wants to control all of Ukraine’s Donbas region.

Moscow’s demands reach beyond Ukraine as well, focusing also on the expansion of NATO.

Russian negotiators proposed in Abu Dhabi that Finland, which joined the alliance in 2023, leave NATO and that the alliance be barred from having military bases in Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, the German newspaper Bild reported on Friday.

The informal proposals, shared with European representatives, also called for arrangements to guarantee freedom of navigation in the Black Sea and the Baltic Sea, Bild reported.

On Thursday, Witkoff and Kushner met Putin in Moscow, where the two sides agreed to continue the talks, before the envoys met Zelenskyy in Ireland.

Why has Ukraine carried out attacks during talks?

“Kyiv continues to demonstrate two points simultaneously: That it is willing to negotiate and that it has a position of strength,” Timtchenko said. “In parallel with any peace talks, Ukraine will likely continue to strike Russia’s military and the sources of funding for Russia’s war machine.”

Ukraine has repeatedly targeted Russian refineries, ports, and energy infrastructure to raise the economic cost of Moscow’s war effort.

But the strikes have drawn criticism from Washington. Trump has blamed Ukraine’s attacks on Russian energy infrastructure for rising diesel prices, and last month he waived sanctions on Russia that Congress had overwhelmingly approved.

Timtchenko said the strikes still gave Kyiv leverage. “Long-range strikes considerably strengthen Ukraine’s hand at the negotiating table, which is why Russian officials keep bringing them up,” he said.

Russia has not commented publicly on the reported strike on its warship.

Governor Drozdenko said 150 drones were shot down over the Leningrad region during Wednesday’s attack, which also cut off a power station.

“Moscow might voice harsh rhetoric and try to blame the Ukrainians for undermining the peace talks,” Timtchenko said. “However, this is nothing new, since Russia has done this numerous times before.

“Despite Moscow’s pretence of seeking an end to the war, Russia continues to strike Ukraine’s military, critical infrastructure, and civilians,” he added.

articles.body: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick agreed to testify before a Senate committee about Nvidia. A Microsoft outage hits millions of users worldwide. And a deadly Washington, D.C., shooting followed a legal feud over mold in a condo. Here’s what to know today. Commerce secretary agrees to testify about Nvidia as national security concerns grow Facing bipartisan pressure, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has agreed to testify before Congress regarding the expanding Nvidia scandal. This is Morning Rundown, a weekday newsletter to start your day. Sign up here to get it in your inbox. The announcement came hours after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned following reports that he had multiple extramarital relationships, including one with a suspected Chinese spy. Earlier Thursday, Republican Sen. Tim Scott, chair of the Senate Banking Committee, sent letters to Lutnick and Huang asking them to “appear voluntarily” at a public hearing. Other lawmakers, including the top Democrats on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, have demanded answers from Lutnick about the Trump administration’s “approval of advanced AI chip exports.” The White House has defended Lutnick and Huang has previously praised the commerce secretary for helping to advance U.S. efforts to maintain its leadership in AI. The scrutiny surrounding Huang gained widespread attention after Nvidia said Sunday that it was investigating whether he had fallen victim to a foreign intelligence operation. Then The New York Times reported on Wednesday that Huang had also had an extramarital relationship with a married Nvidia executive who reported directly to him. More on the mounting political pressure. Related coverage on the Nvidia scandal: Who is Colette Kress? The company’s interim CEO has been its chief financial officer since 2013 and is a familiar face on Wall Street.
