So what happens next? For subscribers: The honey trap, explained: The fake romance tactic stretches as far back as the Bible and has been used to ensnare congressmen and colonels. Microsoft outage hits millions of global users A massive global outage affecting more than a dozen Microsoft cloud services, including Outlook and Teams, stretched into Friday as the tech giant struggled to restore services critical to the daily operations of governments, schools and businesses around the world. In an overnight update, Microsoft said it was “seeing positive results for server stability” and was “not aware of any malicious activity that is causing this incident.” The company had said in updates Wednesday afternoon that it was troubleshooting server problems. Email traffic for many of the tech giant’s 450 million users ground to a halt around midday Wednesday, with email programs freezing or crashing and mobile devices unable to refresh inboxes or send messages. Follow our live coverage. Democrats look to reverse Medicaid and food stamp cuts After taking control of Congress, Democratic leaders in the House and Senate said they would move quickly to reverse cuts to Medicaid and food stamps enacted under President Donald Trump’s “big, beautiful bill.” But they may have to work with the president to get anything through, and his elevation of Stephen Miller to chief of staff has raised questions about his willingness to compromise. Democrats also fall short of the 60 Senate votes needed to overcome a Republican filibuster. Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan had one suggestion for winning the president’s support: Call the initiatives “Trumpcare for All” if that’s what it takes to secure his signature. Policy experts warn that Democrats may have to settle for incremental changes, such as delaying the introduction of work requirements or expanding the list of exemptions. But with millions of people affected by the Trump administration’s changes, activists are urging Democrats to act quickly. The “big, beautiful bill’s” effect on Medicaid and SNAP programs. More politics news: Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland said he will run for Senate majority leader as calls grow for Democrats to select an alternative to Sen. Chuck Schumer. Democrat Sen. Cindy Holscher narrowly won Kansas’ race for governor against Republican state Senate President Ty Masterson. D.C. shooting followed a lengthy legal fight The suspect in Wednesday’s shooting in Washington, D.C., which left one person dead and four others injured, was identified as Matt Lambert, an emergency room doctor embroiled in a lengthy and costly legal battle with his condominium association. Lambert alleged that his home, valued at more than $1 million, had suffered mold and water damage. As the shooting unfolded, one witness said he saw a person fall from a chair with “blood coming from his head.” Others said they did not initially realize what the noise was. After the shooting ended, Lambert was found dead inside his condo from an apparent self-inflicted gunshot wound. The person killed was identified as James Stuart, the building’s manager and a “central fact witness” in Lambert’s lawsuit against the condominium association. Read more about Lambert’s legal feud. Even before Trump’s return to the White House, Cuba was mired in a deep economic crisis with prolonged blackouts and shortages in fuel, medicine and food. With fuel in even more short supply, life has become even more challenging for the average Cuban. We set out to cover the crumbling homes in Havana and were shocked at the dangerous conditions people are living in. Many Cubans remain in unstable homes that are near collapse because they have nowhere else to go and cannot afford costly repairs. We never imagined that people were still living inside some of these decaying buildings. — Carmen Sesin, reporter Read All About It New prostate cancer screening guidelines recommend regular testing for most older men as rates of the disease continue to rise. articles.title: Hamas had far more control over the media’s Gaza coverage than people realize
articles.summary: Photographer Motaz Azaiza was celebrated worldwide for showing Gazans’ suffering. But over the course of the last months, we have since learned how selective he was about what he chose to show. In September, the Palestinian photographer told podcaster Ahmed Biqawi that on Oct. 7, 2023, he encountered a Hamas Qassam Brigades vehicle carrying Israeli…
articles.body:
Photographer Motaz Azaiza was celebrated worldwide for showing Gazans’ suffering. But over the course of the last months, we have since learned how selective he was about what he chose to show.

In September, the Palestinian photographer told podcaster Ahmed Biqawi that on Oct. 7, 2023, he encountered a Hamas Qassam Brigades vehicle carrying Israeli hostages. Residents of Gaza gathered around it, and some began beating the captives. Azaiza followed, filming as he went. But he never published the footage , he explained, fearing Israel would use it to identify and target those involved.

This was an unusual admission from a man whose international reputation rested on his role as an eyewitness to the war. Before Oct. 7, Azaiza had roughly 25,000 Instagram followers. Within months, his audience grew to millions. He reaped the rewards: GQ Middle East named him Man of the Year, TIME included him among the world’s 100 most influential people, and France’s Normandy region awarded him its Liberty Prize.

His photographs documented Gaza’s devastation. What his Western admirers did not know was that he had also recorded evidence of violence against Israelis and deliberately kept it from public view.

That was hardly the only revelation. In the same interview, Azaiza described how journalists in Gaza had grown accustomed to lowering their cameras when residents criticized Hamas. He spoke of a WhatsApp group called Smart , reportedly administered by a Hamas-affiliated media figure, through which journalists communicated.

With the benefit of hindsight, his disclosures reveal a troubling pattern in wartime reporting from Gaza: Information is withheld, criticism suppressed and journalists intimidated into silence.

Western journalists are accustomed to the fog of war, when facts are incomplete, witnesses are traumatized or frightened and independent access is limited. But Azaiza described a far more deliberate process that determines how some information is disseminated and some is suppressed. The photographer had access to evidence, recorded it, and chose to keep it unseen . He also described pressures that could discourage other journalists from publishing or airing criticism of Hamas.

Consider the implications for Western newsrooms that relied heavily on reporting from Gaza. How much did their audiences know about the pressures on those supplying the information? And how carefully did they scrutinize the people presenting themselves as journalists?

A September review by the Committee to Protect Journalists offers another reason to ask. The organization removed 22 individuals from its database of journalists and media workers killed during the conflict — 19 of them were identified as militants or combatants . Some had even been identified as fighters by Hamas or Palestinian Islamic Jihad.

How did people later identified as combatants come to be counted among the journalists killed in the war?

Qatar-based news network Al Jazeera also reportedly dismissed 24 Gaza-based employees amid a lawsuit filed alleging the network provided support to Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad.

Meanwhile, the coverage had an effect on millions of Americans’ judgments about Israel. In 2021 , Gallup found that 58 percent of Americans sympathized more with Israelis than Palestinians, compared to just 25 percent that sympathized more with the Palestinians. By February 2026 , 41 percent expressed greater sympathy for Palestinians and 36 percent for Israelis.

A May Pew survey found increasingly negative American views of both the Israeli government and Israeli people, while views of Palestinians remained comparatively stable.

For three years, Americans consumed images and accounts from a war where the information environment was far less independent than many may have understood. These revelations should prompt a serious examination of the information that reached Western audiences. It should lead to questioning about what was omitted and how confidently news organizations presented information they could not independently verify.

Yet an even more uncomfortable question remains: Is anyone willing to reconsider the story they have already accepted?

Jacki Karsh is a six-time Emmy-nominated multimedia journalist and a board member of the Jewish Federation of Los Angeles.

articles.title: West Lindsey solar project latest to be announced in Lincolnshire
articles.summary: The latest proposals follow a series of major solar development plans across Lincolnshire.
articles.body:
A public consultation has been launched on proposals for a large-scale solar farm in West Lindsey.

Renewable energy developer Elgin said the 99MW Stone Pit Lane Solar Farm, planned on land south of Keelby, could generate enough renewable electricity to power up to 40,000 homes.

The company said it was seeking feedback from residents before submitting a planning application to West Lindsey District Council.

The consultation runs from 12 November to 10 December, with drop-in sessions taking place at Keelby Village Hall on 18 and 19 November.

According to the developer, the scheme would help increase Britain's supply of renewable energy, reduce reliance on imported fossil fuels and support energy security.

The company has also pledged to establish a Community Benefit Fund to support local groups and projects, with ideas from residents welcomed during the consultation.

Senior development manager Jamie Andrews said: "The plans are at an early stage, meaning the design is evolving and local expertise will play an important role in determining the final scheme."

The latest proposals follow a series of major solar development plans across Lincolnshire.

Earlier this year, plans for a solar farm near Keelby and Healing were approved by North East Lincolnshire Council, despite objections from local residents, as well as Healing Parish Council and Keelby Parish Council.

The site is located in two council areas and a planning application has also been approved by West Lindsey District Council, subject to conditions.

Meanwhile, a legal challenge to the UK's largest currently approved solar farm has been rejected by the High Court.

The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) approved Springwell Solar Farm , between Lincoln and Sleaford, in April, saying it would help "bring down bills for good".

Lincolnshire County Council and North Kesteven District Council sought to overturn the decision, arguing the project would harm rural communities and landscapes.

County council leader Sean Matthews said he was "bitterly disappointed" by the outcome.

"We've got to think of food security and this government just don't do that," he said.

"They're just going to be covering more and more of our good, most versatile land with solar panels."

Springwell is classed as a Nationally Significant Infrastructure Project (NSIP) , meaning it required government approval.

Smaller projects can be decided locally.

In August, one farmer told the BBC he had no choice but to turn to solar in order to survive.

Matthews said he was "all for solar panels", adding: "I just don't want them on our farmland."

He said more needed to be done to support struggling farmers to ensure growing crops remained a viable business.

"That's a bigger discussion that we need to have with supermarkets," he added.

articles.title: No regime change, no victory? Trump's Iran endgame & Netanyahu's mission
articles.summary: The war against Iran was never just about its nuclear programme.
articles.body: The war against Iran was never just about its nuclear programme. Even before American and Israeli forces launched their military campaign, Donald Trump was encouraging Iranians to rise against their government, promising that "help is on its way".Now, nearly nine months into the confrontation, the US president has made his ambition even clearer. He says he would consider it a defeat if Iran's ruling regime survives beyond his presidency.In an interview with conservative radio host Hugh Hewitt on Thursday, November 12, Trump was asked whether it would amount to a defeat if Iran's current leadership remained in power when he left office."Yes, that would be a defeat. I would say that would be a defeat. Absolutely," he replied, according to The Times of Israel.The remarks go beyond Trump's earlier warnings about Iran's nuclear and missile capabilities. They put the removal of the Islamic Republic's ruling establishment at the centre of how he measures the outcome of the confrontation, although he did not announce a new plan for achieving regime change.Trump's latest remarks follow months of increasingly explicit calls for the removal of Iran's ruling establishment. In January, when anti-government protests spread across Iran, he publicly urged demonstrators to continue their movement and take control of government institutions."Iranian Patriots, KEEP PROTESTING - TAKE OVER YOUR INSTITUTIONS!!!" Trump wrote in a January 13 post on Truth Social. "HELP IS ON ITS WAY," he added, without explaining what assistance he was promising.Reuters reported that Trump also said he had cancelled meetings with Iranian officials until the alleged killing of protesters stopped. His remarks drew a sharp response from Tehran, which accused Washington of encouraging political destabilisation and interfering in Iran's internal affairs.Trump made his position more explicit on February 28, when the United States and Israel launched their joint military campaign against Iran.In his address announcing the operation, Trump urged members of Iran's armed forces and security agencies to surrender, while telling the public that the opportunity to overthrow the government had arrived.Trump is not alone in seeking regime change, Israel has long wanted Iran's rulers goneFor Israel, the objective of the war against Iran goes beyond crippling its nuclear programme and destroying its missile capabilities.Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has long viewed the Islamic Republic as an existential threat to Israel, accusing its leadership of pursuing nuclear weapons, building a regional network of armed groups and maintaining an ideological commitment to Israel's destruction.Netanyahu made his position explicit on February 28, when Israel and the US launched their joint military campaign. In a televised address, he said the operation was aimed at ending the threat posed by Iran's ruling establishment and creating conditions for Iranians to overthrow their government.Israel's concerns centre on four interconnected issues. The first is Iran's nuclear programme, which Netanyahu has repeatedly described as an existential danger.Israel fears that Tehran could eventually develop a nuclear weapon while retaining the ballistic missile capabilities to deliver it.The second is Iran's missile arsenal, which can threaten Israeli cities and military installations. The third is Tehran's support for regional armed groups, including Hezbollah in Lebanon, Hamas in Gaza and the Houthis in Yemen, which Israel considers part of an Iranian network of influence directed against it.The fourth is the ideological hostility of Iran's clerical leadership towards Israel. Netanyahu has repeatedly accused the Islamic Republic of seeking Israel's destruction, arguing that weakening its military capabilities without changing its political leadership would leave the underlying threat intact.Netanyahu's ambition to see the Iranian regime fall was further underlined on October 21, when he explicitly called for its overthrow and said he had given the directive to Israel's military and intelligence agencies."There is only one way to remove this threat once and for all: overthrow the regime in Iran," he said at an Israeli military officer graduation ceremony, according to The Washington Post.Yet, the biggest question for Trump and Netanyahu is whether military victory can translate into political change.Eliminating Iran's nuclear infrastructure, weakening its missile arsenal and killing senior leadership may undermine the Islamic Republic, but none of these guarantees its collapse. Iran's powerful security apparatus and governing institutions remain formidable obstacles to an uprising or a transition of power.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Disney alum David Henrie draws firm line on Hollywood intimate scenes that 'violate' his marriage
articles.summary: Actor David Henrie revealed on "The Unplanned Podcast" that he refuses nudity, sex scenes and kissing roles out of respect for his marriage.
articles.body: Actor David Henrie drew a firm line regarding his Hollywood career, saying he refuses to take on roles involving nudity, sex scenes or kissing out of respect for his marriage. "For me, I draw the line if it’s anything that would actually violate our relationship as a married couple," Henrie told Matt and Abby Howard’s "The Unplanned Podcast" on Tuesday. Appearing alongside his wife, Maria Cahill, the "Wizards of Waverly Place" alum, 37, outlined his acting boundaries, specifically citing "nudity" before Cahill chimed in with a laugh. ANGEL STUDIOS DRAWS LINE IN SAND WITH HOLLYWOOD, BANS SEX SCENES, PROFANITY IN BOLD NEW PLEDGE "He's not kissing anybody," she said. Cahill, who married Henrie in 2017, suggested her husband is more concerned about such scenes than she is, emphasizing the trust she has in him. "I feel like he cares more than I care," she said. "I so trust him, I literally don’t care. He's like, 'I will not kiss [someone else],'" she added. Henrie explained that his general rule is to accept roles as long as they do not conflict with his conscience or personal values, drawing a distinction between portraying fictional wrongdoing and performing intimate scenes. "If I have to kill someone, like, I’m not really killing someone, you know? You can fake that," he explained. MICHAEL DOUGLAS GETS EXPLICIT ABOUT HOW HE FILMED SEX SCENES BEFORE INTIMACY COORDINATORS "[With intimate scenes] you’re not faking that ... You’re really doing that thing ... You’re in bed making out ..." he added later. "I don’t care how much you’re thinking of bees and birds, or whatever you’re doing to distract yourself. You’re really doing that." Henrie said performing such scenes would "feel weird," retierating, "I'm not going to do it." The conversation also turned to Henrie's time playing Justin Russo on Disney Channel's "Wizards of Waverly Place," when he filmed a kissing scene with his character's love interest years before marrying Cahill. The couple recalled how their four children reacted after watching the episode, prompting questions about why he was showing affection to someone other than their mother. "They were like, ‘You have another wife?’ Like, they were so upset," Cahill laughed. "They’ll randomly bring it up, like, ‘Papa kissed another woman,’" Henrie added. "And they’ll go up to her and be like, ‘Papa has a girlfriend.’ It’s so funny." 'ANT-MAN' STAR EVANGELINE LILLY SAYS SHE LEFT HOLLYWOOD BECAUSE SHE 'ALWAYS HATED BEING FAMOUS' Henrie, a devout Catholic, has been open about his faith and the repercussions of his commitment to Christ while acting in Hollywood. During an appearance on the "Bryce Crawford Podcast" earlier this year, Henrie was asked what his faith cost him regarding his career. "It was rough, lost my agents," he said. "I walked away from a lot. I turned down a lot of roles. I was like I'm just not going to do something that I think will disrespect my belief now or disrespect our Lord. I'm just not going to do it. I'm not going to go near it. And it cost me a lot. It cost a lot. I lost a lot of money. Friends, a girlfriend at the time. I kind of was stripped of everyone, everyone that I would call a friend." Henrie added that he made new friends that challenged him, which eventually led to him meeting his wife. articles.title: Paris court annuls Sotheby’s sale of Pissarro painting
articles.summary: A French court has annulled a Sotheby’s sale of a Camille Pissarro painting and ordered the auction house to help the descendants of the artwork’s original Jewish owner.
articles.body: A French court has annulled a Sotheby’s sale of a Camille Pissarro painting and ordered the auction house to help the descendants of the artwork’s original Jewish owner. “Darse de pêche et bassin Duquesne, Dieppe, après-midi ensoleillée” (“Fishing dock and Duquesne basin, Dieppe, sunny afternoon”) fetched £1.2 million (roughly $1.6 million) when it was sold by the London branch of the auction house in 2024 to an anonymous buyer, according to the court ruling. Salomon Flavian, a Jewish banker of French and Romanian heritage, was featured in the provenance section of the painting’s listing on Sotheby’s website because he bought the painting in 1935, the court stated. There was little else on the listing to explain that the painting was looted during World War II, however the listing did include a single line stating: “This work is being offered for sale pursuant to a settlement between the current owner and heirs of Salomon Flavian.” According to background in the court ruling sent to CNN, two of the Flavian descendants reached an agreement with the seller in 2024. But other descendants later brought a lawsuit over the sale, arguing that they had not been party to that agreement. But last week a French court ruled in favor of those descendants. Salomon Flavian, a Jewish banker of French and Romanian heritage, bought the 1902 landscape in 1935, according to the ruling. When war broke out in September 1939, he arranged for the painting and dozens of others to be stored in crates at the Westminster Foreign Bank in Paris. Those crates, with the Pissarro painting inside, were seized by the Nazis in 1941, the ruling said. After the war, Flavian — who survived — was reunited with some of his looted artwork, but some works, including the Pissarro, were never restituted to the family, according to the ruling. Reaching its judgment on November 5, the Paris Judicial Court annulled the sale and ordered Sotheby’s to “disclose the full identity of the buyer of the work” within two months in order to enable its return to the family. Furthermore, it said that if Sotheby’s does not disclose the buyer’s identity within the two-month period it will be liable to pay a 1,000 euro ($1,115) penalty for every additional day that it fails to do so. The court also ruled against the Toronto-based Mondex Corporation, a firm specializing in the return of Nazi-looted art. According to background in the court ruling sent to CNN, Mondex assisted with the agreement reached between the painting’s seller and two of the Flavian descendants. The court ruled against Mondex for its role in the agreement reached between Sotheby’s, the seller and the two Flavian descendants it was representing. It was ordered to pay the descendants 10,000 euros (around $11,000). Mondex Corporation maintains the painting was not looted and that British art collector Edward Le Bas was the owner from 1939 to the early 1950s. In a statement sent to CNN, it said: “We understand that the court’s decision was lacking a detailed analysis of the provenance evidence provided and as such warrants an appeal so that all of the relevant facts can be considered thoroughly.” Following the ruling, the Flavian descendants who brought the case issued a statement through the law firm representing them, Cabinet Corinne Hershkovitch. They said: “The heirs of Salomon Flavian are pleased that the Paris Court of Justice has recognized the spoliation of the claimed Pissarro painting and, through this historic ruling, has restored the memory and honor of their father and grandfather. “ In a statement sent to CNN Friday, Sotheby’s said: “While we respect its judgment regarding the restitution of Pissarro’s Darse de pêche et bassin Duquesne, we are disappointed by this aspect of the decision. The history of the artwork is complex. We fully recognise the profound losses suffered by the Flavian family during the Nazi era and, from the outset, have approached this matter responsibly and with the care and respect it deserves.” Sotheby’s went on to say: “There is a procedural process that will need to be followed in order for this aspect of the decision to be enforced in the UK, and we are reviewing the judgment in detail.” The action was taken against the UK arm of Sotheby’s by a French court because the spoliation of Flavian’s private collection had occurred in Nazi-occupied Paris. Nans Méger is a partner at Cabinet Corinne Hershkovitch, the law firm that represents the Flavian heirs. He told CNN: “There are established legal procedures for the recognition and enforcement of foreign judgments, and we are confident in our ability to pursue them successfully.” “We will take all necessary legal steps to protect our clients’ interests and secure the restitution of the painting, just as we have done consistently since the proceedings began in 2024.” He added: “It would also be important to highlight that the judgment is based on the French Ordinance of 21 April 1945, which itself stems from the 1943 Inter-Allied Declaration of London, and provides for the nullity of transactions involving property looted during the Nazi Occupation.” “The Court also expressly referred to the 1998 Washington Principles on Nazi-Confiscated Art, endorsed by 44 countries, which, although non-binding, established an international framework for addressing Nazi-era art looting and seeking just and fair solutions.” Despite it being more than 80 years since the end of World War II, the issue of looted art remains a hot topic. The Nazi regime orchestrated the largest art theft in world history between 1933 and 1945, seizing more than 650,000 works of art across Europe from Jewish families, collectors and museums, according to the Center for Art Law.

articles.title: Nvidia scandal: What’s next for the US tech company?
articles.summary: What happens next at one of the world’s most valuable companies will have repercussions far beyond Silicon Valley.
articles.body:
The departure of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, the 63-year-old cofounder and face of the chipmaking company which has become the backbone of the modern AI industry, has shaken the US’s Silicon Valley.

Nvidia, valued at nearly $4 trillion, is a critical pillar of the US economy where AI and tech companies make up some 40 percent of stock market valuations. The furore over Huang’s extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy, has wiped hundreds of billions of dollars from the company’s market value, dragging down the S&P 500 and Nasdaq.

While CFO Colette Kress has temporarily stepped into the top job at Nvidia, the search for cofounder Huang’s successor continues.

What happens next at one of the world’s most valuable companies will have repercussions far beyond Silicon Valley. So, what’s next for Nvidia?

On October 29, The New York Times reported that US intelligence agencies suspected a Chinese businesswoman and executive associated with Singapore-based AI infrastructure company Megaspeed International, Alice Huang, had been tapped by China’s Ministry of State Security to gather information from Nvidia’s Huang.

The newspaper reported that the two were involved in an intimate relationship, later confirmed by the cofounder of the company in an internal memo. Nvidia’s board launched an independent investigation into whether Huang had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation.

“I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry,” Huang wrote in an internal memo to Nvidia staff.

The business links go beyond just the affair, however, fuelling further concerns. Megaspeed purchased more than $4.8bn of Nvidia chips over roughly two years. Separately, The Information reported that Alice Huang facilitated at least $7.5bn in Nvidia chip shipments to Chinese firms, raising even more questions about skirting US export controls.

Then, on Wednesday, the NYT reported a second alleged affair between Jensen Huang and Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare, who reported directly to him.

The next day, Huang was forced out of the company and off its board.

Hours later, Reuters reported that Huang had allegedly been involved in a third affair with another Nvidia employee, citing two people familiar with the matter.

In simple terms, if Nvidia sneezes, the AI industry and modern computing catch a cold.

Nvidia controls nearly 90 percent of the market for advanced AI chips which are used to train frontier AI models, giving it an extraordinary degree of influence over the global AI industry and the infrastructure powering it.

Observers say the company holds the keys to next-generation computing. Its customers include tech giants such as Microsoft, Google, Amazon and Meta, which rely on Nvidia hardware to build and operate their AI data centres.

That’s also why Washington has restricted Nvidia from selling chips to China.

Nvidia’s Huang has spent years lobbying in Washington against such restrictions, arguing that restricting sales would surrender a strategically important market to domestic Chinese competitors.

That puts him at odds with US lawmakers who view access to Nvidia’s advanced chips as a national security risk, particularly given their potential military applications.

A Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson said Beijing has “always opposed the abuse of export control measures”, as pressure gains momentum yet again in Washington. Beijing has rejected allegations that Alice Huang is a Chinese spy as “baseless”.

In China, investors have been selling shares in Chinese AI-linked companies over worries that recent developments at Nvidia could deepen the technological divide between Beijing and Washington.

On Friday, shares in Z.AI, one of China’s top AI model developers, tumbled more than 10 percent in Hong Kong while shares in rival MiniMax hit record lows.

A Reuters review identified more than $3bn in Chinese computing projects built around Nvidia’s restricted processors – despite the American chipmaker claiming that US export controls effectively shut it out of the AI data-centre market in the world’s second-biggest economy.

The examination shows projects stretching from China’s wealthy coastal technology hubs to remote western provinces, and underscores how deeply Nvidia’s technology remains embedded in China’s AI expansion.

Nvidia shares rose 1.8 percent in premarket trading on Friday after losing around 11 percent of their value this week up to Thursday, when Huang exited the company he built.

The company is on course for its longest streak of weekly losses since October 2012.

US President Donald Trump is scheduled to meet his Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, next week in Shenzhen at the APEC leaders’ summit.

Similarly, shares in Nvidia’s customers, such as South Korea’s Naver, fell more than 5 percent. Nasdaq futures and S&P 500 futures fell 0.4 percent and 0.15 percent, respectively.

“Jensen has obviously been a singular force in many ways so the impact will likely be felt far and wide,” UBS analyst Timothy Arcuri told Reuters.

“The company has become a key source of funds for a host of AI industry participants including neo-clouds, LLM developers, ecosystem partners, and suppliers, and we have always seen Jensen as a key driving force for this effort,” Arcuri said.

“Even if a new leader ultimately maintains a similar approach, there is likely to be some ‘pause’ in the company’s willingness and ability to continue pursuing these deals in the near term,” he added.

From washing dishes at a Denny’s to building a $4 trillion technology giant, Huang has led Nvidia for nearly 33 years – and made one of Silicon Valley’s defining entrepreneurial stories.

But the “cult-style” leaders at Silicon Valley – including Huang, Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg and Elon Musk – also reflect the concentration of market power that tech companies enjoy. Technology stocks now account for nearly 40 percent of the S&P 500’s total market value.

That is likely to rise when AI companies Anthropic and OpenAI also go public.

And in the absence of a clear succession plan, things could go awry, sending jitters among investors – a concern which Nvidia highlighted itself in its annual review for this year.

Under the risk factors dealing with its dependence on key personnel, Nvidia’s report noted that the company is “highly dependent on the services of our longstanding executive team”.

“Failure to ensure effective succession planning, transfer of knowledge, and smooth transitions involving executives and key employees could hinder our strategic planning, execution, and long-term success,” it said.

Nvidia’s board has begun searching for a permanent successor to Huang, tapping CFO Kress as interim CEO.

Meanwhile, President Trump, who has defended Huang as a “genius”, shared his two cents, too. He suggested former Apple chief executive Tim Cook could take over Nvidia. “A Legend replaces a Legend,” Trump wrote.

Nvidia has said it will consider candidates from both within and outside the company.

articles.title: Moscow car explosion injures former aide to pro-Russian Ukrainian politician
articles.summary: A car explosion in southern Moscow injured a former aide to a pro-Russian Ukrainian politician on Friday, according to Russian authorities, the second apparent attack in two days.
articles.body: A car explosion in southern Moscow injured a former aide to a pro-Russian Ukrainian politician on Friday, according to Russian authorities, the second apparent attack in two days. Sergey Zavorotny, who served as an adviser to the former pro-Russian prime minister of Ukraine Mykola Azarov, was transported to a city hospital for medical care, the Investigative Committee of Russia for the city of Moscow said in a statement. Azarov served as the Ukrainian prime minister from 2010 to 2014, when he fled to Russia during the street protests known as the Maidan Revolution. The Russian Investigative Committee said that a comprehensive investigation into the explosion on Moscow’s Kirovogradskaya Street is underway. Video from the scene shows a dark gray SUV that has been heavily damaged, with the windows apparently blown out. It’s the latest in a series of apparent attacks or assassinations against political and military figures inside Russia. On Thursday, a car explosion in St. Petersburg killed a Russian serviceman, the local Investigative Committee said. Russia has blamed Ukraine for earlier assassinations of military officials. Ukrainian authorities have not commented on this week’s explosions. The latest incidents come amid the United States’ latest diplomatic efforts to end Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff met with both Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and Russia’s Vladimir Putin this week, and announced that European delegates will join the next round of peace talks. The pair had flown to Moscow after trilateral talks between the US, Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi this week concluded with no clear breakthrough. After speaking to Putin in Moscow, Kushner said: “Both sides have now agreed to expand the next round of negotiations to include our European partners.” This is a developing story and will be updated.

articles.title: Ukraine claims record 3,000 Russian casualties in one day as war drags on
articles.summary: Meanwhile, Russia appears to suggest it has control of half of unoccupied Donbas.
articles.body:
As Ukraine, Russia and the United States engaged in their first peace talks since February this week, the front lines continued to deteriorate for Moscow as its casualties rose to a possible new record without any significant territorial gains.

Ukraine’s military said it had caused more than 26,000 Russian casualties – meaning those killed and seriously wounded – in the first 10 days of November, suggesting this month’s figure could mark a new record topping October’s 54,400.

On November 9, Ukraine also claimed a new daily record of 2,980 Russian soldiers killed or wounded. That marked the fourth reported daily record this year.

Al Jazeera cannot independently verify casualty claims by either side.

This cluster of new casualty records in the autumn, accompanied by a lack of any significant territorial gains by Russia, suggested that Moscow was not coming any closer to its goal of seizing the last remaining quarter of Ukraine’s eastern Donbas region this year.

A group of pro-Ukrainian hackers from Belarus said they had accessed records of the Russian state statistical service, Rosstat, and discovered an official tally of 450,000 Russian fatalities for the entire full-scale invasion, since 2022.

Independent assessments indicate that Russia has seized a net 117sq km (45sq miles) this year, a poor showing for its pains.

Yet, Russia was as defiant as ever at peace talks in Abu Dhabi on November 10-11.

Presidential aide Vladimir Medinsky, who headed the Russian delegation, told Vesti television after the talks concluded that he would be satisfied “only when we win and sign a peace agreement on our terms”.

Russia has demanded territory Ukraine is not willing to surrender, and said NATO needs to pull out of all the former Soviet bloc countries which joined it since 1997.

Medinsky called for “a new, comprehensive, and just security system in Europe,” because the one put in place after World War II “is functioning very poorly, and, in fact, the entire system is sick. In Ukraine, a festering wound has simply burst.”

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy saw it differently.

“When the Russians now talk about a security architecture for themselves … What they really want is to freely interfere in the affairs of other countries, and to use force whenever they want, and to make sure that no one can support liberty inside Russia,” he told the Danish parliament, the Folketing, on the day the talks concluded.

Although US negotiators agreed to table the subject of a European security architecture at Abu Dhabi, the three European powers present – Germany, France and the United Kingdom – did not, and they were excluded from the proceedings.

“We did not communicate with them. We don’t really understand what their status is here,” Medinsky said.

Europe agrees with Ukraine that such a discussion puts the cart before the horse.

“The idea of discussing European-Russian security infrastructure is a complex and potentially dangerous one,” Zelenskyy said on the eve of the talks. “First, we must discuss how to end Russia’s war against Ukraine. Second, what the security infrastructure will be for Ukraine.”

Ukraine has asked for an ironclad guarantee of military intervention if it is attacked again, as offered in NATO’s Article 5.

Instead, Zelenskyy said, the Trump administration offered “something similar to NATO”.

Russian President Vladimir Putin received the US negotiating team in Saint Petersburg after talks in Abu Dhabi, and repeated the Russian position that the presence of European peacekeepers in a post-war Ukraine would also be “absolutely unacceptable”.

Zelenskyy attributed Russia’s absolutism to its inaccurate understanding of realities on the ground.

“Putin lives in a different reality,” he told journalists in Copenhagen on November 11. “When I received the second report from our negotiating group after the meetings in Abu Dhabi, they told me that the Russians believe and claim that they have already occupied half of the [part of the] Donbas region which is actually under our control. These were military officers, Russian intelligence.”

Russia’s defence ministry has claimed to have seized 3,600sq km (1,400sq miles) of Ukraine this year, and Putin has repeated the claim.

Still, Abu Dhabi did produce some results.

Russia and Ukraine said there would be a new POW exchange of at least 1,000 or possibly 1,500 prisoners on each side. And Zelenskyy said de-escalation steps were discussed.

In the run-up to Abu Dhabi, Russia pounded Ukraine’s cities.

“For 10 days and nights, Ukraine faced constant alarms,” said its General Staff. During that period, Russia launched 3,519 drones, and Ukraine managed to intercept 3,068 of them, they said, including 83 percent of the jet-powered drones, which now comprise roughly half of the swarm.

On the night of November 7, Russia unleashed 36 ballistic missiles into Ukraine, including some reportedly manufactured by North Korea, striking energy infrastructure.

Prime Minister Serhiy Koretskyi has asked European allies to provide generators and battery packs for homes, as well as mobile shelters and buses to keep urban transport moving during blackouts.

On November 12, Ukraine reported it was experiencing renewed restrictions on its use of the Starlink satellite service, which it needs to coordinate interceptors to incoming Russian drones.

“This directly impacts our ability to intercept Russian kamikaze drones,” said Zelenskyy. “Due to the speed limitations, we simply cannot intercept them in time.”

This came as Ukraine continued its own strikes inside Russia, targeting ballistic missile launchers and factories as a forward defence.

On November 7, a fire burned almost a hectare of storage space next to an Almaz factory in Rostov, which makes communications equipment. It was unclear whether Ukraine caused it. On the same day, Ukraine fired Neptune missiles into the Proton-Electrotex conglomerate which makes parts for Kormoran cruise and Iskander ballistic missiles, and destroyed two ballistic missile launchers.

On November 9, Ukraine struck the Morozov plant near St Petersburg, which makes solid rocket fuel for ballistic missiles, and the Redkino plant in Tver, which makes chemical products used in missiles.

On November 10, Ukraine struck the 123rd Aircraft Repair Plant in Novgorod, which services Russia’s increasingly rare A-50 early warning and targeting aircraft.

On November 11, Ukraine struck the Naro-Forminsk cruiser, which launches Kalibr and Onyx cruise missiles.

“We are acting asymmetrically,” Ukrainian defence minister Yevhenii Khmara told his Dutch counterpart. Ukraine had struck a total of 12 ballistic missile launch sites inside Russia, he said without specifying the timeframe, and said the strikes on factories were reducing Russian production capacity.

Zelenskyy renewed his call for German Taurus missiles with which to strike Russian launchers.

Ukraine also struck a series of refineries during the past week, including the Afipsky, Saratov, Kirishi, Ust-Luga and Omsk refineries. Russian military reporters said three Russian helicopters had been downed by friendly fire during attempts to defend the Ust-Luga refinery.

Since the end of October, its General Staff said, Ukraine had struck Russia’s five biggest refineries.

Sources told Reuters that Ukraine has destroyed at least 30 percent of Russia’s refining capacity.

The purpose of refinery strikes is to diminish Russian export revenue for petroleum products and to disrupt its economy. Those goals appeared to be working last week, as Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service reported Moscow projecting a $63bn-$67bn deficit for 2026, double its intended figure, and Russian media reported staff layoffs at the parliament, or Duma, and the Russian Federation Council.

articles.title: Can Netanyahu launch a strike on Iran before he leaves?
articles.summary: PM’s caretaker government can legally go to war, though it would likely inflame domestic divisions.
articles.body:
Despite losing its majority in last month’s parliamentary elections, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s government is still in power in a caretaker capacity.

That will continue until a new governing majority is formed – a process that could take months as Israel’s opposition struggles to form a coalition.

And while he may be politically weakened, Netanyahu is reported to be weighing new military action against Iran , despite a lack of enthusiasm from the United States, his own military establishment, and the politicians vying to replace him.

But does Netanyahu’s caretaker government actually have the authority to send Israel back to war, and how would such a move be received at home?

What military options does Israel’s caretaker government have?

Officially, Israel’s caretaker government has the same authority as a regular government. Article 30 of the country’s Basic Law states that an interim government continues to carry out the same duties until a new one takes its place.

However, Israel’s Supreme Court has previously ruled that an outgoing government must avoid irreversible policy moves unless they are urgent – a principle known as the “duty of restraint”.

In practice, Netanyahu can still initiate military action with the approval of his caretaker government, which he could present as “urgent and in the national interest”, Neve Gordon, a professor of international law at Queen Mary University, London, and the author of “Israel’s Occupation”, told Al Jazeera.

Or Asher, a researcher at the Tel Aviv-based Tachlith Institute, told the Reuters news agency that security issues generally are “the clearest exception” to a caretaker government’s duty of restraint.

“The Supreme Court has historically avoided intervening in decisions to go to war, and parliamentary oversight is at its thinnest in the weeks after the new Knesset [parliament] ⁠⁠convenes and before its committees are formed,” said Asher.

“A caretaker prime minister can legally take Israel to war, including against Iran,” he added.

Ehab Jabareen, an analyst and Palestinian citizen of Israel, told Al Jazeera the government’s caretaker status raises the “political burden of proof”.

“Netanyahu would be asking the country to accept the consequences of a decision that could outlast his government,” he said.

Is Netanyahu pushing for a return to war with Iran?

On Wednesday, Israeli media reported that the security cabinet chaired by Netanyahu had ordered the military to step up preparations for an attack on Iran.

“The directives issued by the security cabinet to the Israeli military could lead it to carry out activities that could trigger a war,” public broadcaster KAN reported.

That followed reports that Netanyahu has been repeatedly calling US President Donald Trump to press for a new military campaign against Iran, conversations that on at least one occasion became heated, according to Israel’s Ynet News site.

On Thursday, a US military official was quoted by KAN as saying that Washington had told Israel to get ready for a potential new round of confrontation. But the US military’s Central Command (CENTCOM) later dismissed the reports, telling Al Jazeera they were “mere speculation”.

According to Israel’s Channel 13, the Israeli military establishment sees no urgent need to attack Iran. It said that assessment had been presented to Netanyahu and opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, who has been tasked with forming the next government, during a briefing on Wednesday.

The opposition has demanded that Netanyahu avoid any military action unless it is critical.

Yisrael Beytenu leader Avigdor Lieberman, a member of the opposition bloc, said the prime minister’s caretaker government must not “make decisions that could drag Israel into war without parliamentary oversight and without the full agreement of all security officials”.

Eisenkot echoed this sentiment in a letter to Netanyahu on Wednesday, saying that deploying Israeli forces “without a direct and immediate threat that cannot wait could have devastating consequences for Israeli democracy and public trust in the institutions of government”.

The Israeli premier responded by insisting the government makes all decisions based only on “security considerations”.

How would Israeli parties and the public react to renewed war?

“Obviously, those who voted for Netanyahu and parties from his coalition would be in favour, while most of those who supported the so-called change bloc would be upset at Netanyahu’s use of the war to try to remain in power and block their electoral success,” said Gordon.

But ultimately, he said, most people who voted against Netanyahu’s bloc would “rally around the flag” if he resumes hostilities.

Jabareen agreed that Israelis would likely rally if a new war breaks out and missiles are incoming. But he said that “tells you very little about whether they think Netanyahu was right to start another round [of conflict]”.

“And the harder test comes when reservists are called up again, families are back in shelters and the government has to explain what the campaign can achieve that the previous one didn’t,” he added.

Jabareen said the debate in Israel over any new confrontation on Iran would likely centre on “why now?”

“If the case for urgency is weak, especially if Washington is opposed and senior Israeli commanders have reservations, the decision could be seen as an attempt to change the political agenda while Eisenkot is trying to form a government,” he said.

Beyond domestic considerations, an obstacle to Netanyahu restarting attacks may be the position of Israel’s main ally, the US, which has said it is doubling down on its economic pressure campaign against Iran rather than pursuing more large-scale military action.

“Netanyahu’s problem … is not the Israeli public, but what seems to be a loss of appetite in the US,” said Gordon.

Anders Persson, a political scientist specialising in the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, said it would be easier for Netanyahu to pull off a new military campaign if it is undertaken jointly with the US.

But “the more openly Netanyahu provokes Iran, and the less support he receives from Trump, the harder it will be for him to get away with it – and for the Israeli public to accept it”, Persson told Al Jazeera.

Has an Israeli caretaker government previously launched military action?

Yes. And in one case, the government was led by Netanyahu himself.

In May 2021, weeks after his party lost seats in legislative elections and while negotiations for a new government were under way, the prime minister launched an 11-day war in Gaza that killed at least 260 people in the Palestinian enclave. Thirteen people also died in Israel.

While that conflict temporarily stalled efforts to replace Netanyahu, a new government, led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, was formed the following month, ending a 12-year run as prime minister .

Former Israeli prime ministers Ehud Olmert and Yair Lapid also ordered military action in Gaza while serving in a caretaker capacity. The 2008 war directed by Olmert was by far the most deadly , killing about 1,400 Palestinians.

articles.title: Pope Leo makes emotional return to his ‘beloved diocese of Chiclayo’
articles.summary: Pope Leo XIV made a triumphant return to the Peruvian city of Chiclayo, where he served as bishop for and was affectionately nicknamed “Padre Roberto.”
articles.body: LIMA, Peru — Pope Leo XIV made a triumphant return Friday to the Peruvian city of Chiclayo, where he served as bishop for eight years and was affectionately nicknamed “Padre Roberto.” Leo arrived in a plane decorated with “#LeoXFliesHome” stickers and he was greeted with a sign at the airport bearing the same message. A small dance troupe performed before him as he stepped off the plane. He will stay in the area until Sunday to lead eight events, including a private dinner with the priests who once reported to him as bishop. The crowds greeting Leo in Peru’s fourth largest city will likely be smaller than the estimated 3 million or so who welcomed the pope when he arrived Wednesday in Lima, the country’s capital. But their enthusiasm more than made up for their smaller numbers as the former Bishop Robert Prevost of Chiclayo returned to this coastal city of nearly 700,000 as the leader of the Catholic Church. As toured in an open-air popemobile at the Pampas de Pimentel, a vast desert plain just outside Chiclayo, the crowd erupted in cheers, many waving waved white-and-yellow Vatican flags. Some had been waiting since last night to catch a glimpse of the pontiff, many of them forced to walk as lines of cars had blocked the roads where vendors sold hats, mini pope dolls and sweet Peruvian bread. Maria Esther Chozo Reyes, 76, said she had taken a 12-hour bus ride from Lima and arrived Thursday afternoon before she camped overnight. “He knows the people of Chiclayo and he’s lived here, he’s made his mission here,” she told The Associated Press. “We really need his blessing.” Thanking the people for their love and support, in his sermon Leo said it was a blessing to be in his former home. “As I look at your faces, a prayer ⁠of thanksgiving to the Lord arises in my heart for the blessing you have been and continue to be in my life,” he said, adding that his lung cancer disgnosis and surgery to remove part of one lung exactly a month ago had been a time of trial. Leo’s sojourn to Chiclayo is midway through the final leg of his 12-day visit to South America, a historic trip that included stops in Argentina and Uruguay. And it’s the most sentimental part of his journey. For while Leo was born in Chicago and English is his mother tongue, the first words he uttered from the balcony of St. Peter’s Basilica was a shoutout in Spanish to his “beloved Diocese of Chiclayo.” During his time in that city, Leo often repeated a joke: “Chicago, Chiclayo, what difference is there? Only one letter.” Setting aside the fact that it’s actually two letters, Leo quickly became a beloved figure in Chiclayo by championing social justice issues, embracing the poor and venturing into the local prison to say Mass. During the pandemic, Leo endeared himself to many by launching a fundraising drive to raise money for a badly-needed oxygen production plant. When Cyclone Maku hit the area in March 2023, Leo was photographed wading through the floodwaters to get supplies to the destitute and distributing food at soup kitchens. At Christmastime, Leo would drive a pickup truck laden with gifts into remote villages around Chiclayo and join family celebrations. Leo spent two decades as a missionary, priest and finally as a bishop in Peru and became a citizen in 2015. During his two decades in the country, he was also a strident critic of then- Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori’s authoritarian regime. On Thursday, Leo delivered a speech while sitting beside Fujimori’s daughter, recently-elected Peruvian President Keiko Fujimori, at Lima’s Gran Teatro Nacional performing arts center. Leo urged the country’s leaders to cultivate honesty and integrity to strengthen public trust --- and called on officeholders to listen to their constituents. “Today I understand how much of this land remains with me and how much of my own story also belongs to you,” Leo said. There was thunderous applause when Leo referred to Peru as “my homeland.” And Leo appeared to have tears in his eyes as he sang the Peruvian national anthem along with a children’s choir. Claudio Lavanga reported from Lima and Corky Siemaszko from New York.

articles.title: Reform and Tory spokesmen in angry clash over immigration at Piddington
articles.summary: Reform's Zia Yusuf and Tory Chris Philp were speaking against converting a former military site into asylum accommodation.
articles.body:
Conservative MP Chris Philp and Reform UK's Zia Yusuf had a blazing row at a joint press conference, as they joined villagers protesting against asylum accommodation plans.

The pair clashed when sharing a platform in Piddington to oppose converting a former military site at MoD Bicester into accommodation for more than 1,200 detained asylum seekers.

The two politicians were invited to make speeches about the plans, but things became heated after Yusuf asked Philp to apologise for the Conservatives' record on immigration.

Philp, the shadow home secretary, told Yusuf to "calm down" and accused him of "cheap politics", an assertion Reform's home affairs spokesman dismissed.

Asylum centre on military base near Piddington approved

A press conference led by Piddington Parish Council chairman Tim McNally took place on Friday after Housing Secretary Angela Rayner approved the Home Office's application to change the use of the site for asylum accommodation.

The Home Office said this would allow it to continue developing the plan but that no final decision on the site had been taken.

There has been significant local opposition to the proposal and a legal challenge to the planning decision is expected from the parish council.

In September, Piddington symbolically voted to leave the UK over the planned use for the site in Oxfordshire.

Politicians from the Conservatives and Reform have made several visits to Piddington, a village of about 350 people, to show their support for campaigners.

Speaking on Friday, Philp said a future Conservative government would shut the asylum accommodation "straight away" if it was opened by Labour.

Yusuf made clear Reform's opposition to the plans before his focus switched to the Conservatives.

He said: "It's obviously true that we would not be gathered here today and 1,200 men would not be being dumped into this beautiful village were it not for the actions of the Conservative government.

"So I actually want to ask you Chris, would you actually like to apologise for the things you did in government to bring hundreds of thousands of people into this country illegally?"

Philp, a former immigration minister, described Yusuf's remarks as "disingenuous" and argued the migrants who could be housed near Piddington will have arrived in the country while Labour has been in power.

He said the Conservatives are under new leadership and he hoped the politicians could "stand in solidarity with the residents" rather than "engage in point scoring".

Philp added: "Zia, read the room, listen to the people clapping and read the room."

Yusuf countered that it was "important that we hold everybody accountable for this situation" and said Philp had been "heavily involved in immigration and borders policy" for the Conservatives in government.

Philp repeated his "read the room" suggestion, adding: "The public here want you to pipe down on the cheap politics."

Yusuf dismissed the suggestion that he was engaging in "cheap politics" and repeated his criticism of the Conservatives' record, saying they "refused" to secure the country's borders when in power.

As Yusuf spoke, Philp could be heard saying: "Buddy, I'm not here to give you comms advice, mate, you're in a hole stop digging."

Philp told Yusuf he should "calm down", with the Reform politician repeating his request for the Conservative MP to "apologise to the British people".

McNally thanked the pair for attending the press conference, adding: "I understand this is a passionate discussion and I respect you both for what you've got to do and what you represent."

While the two parties are on the right of politics, it is unusual for them to share a platform to campaign and both are keen to stress their differences to voters.

Reform leader Nigel Farage has pitched the party as replacing the "old, fuddy-duddy" Conservatives , and Tory leader Kemi Badenoch has said she would rather have another general election than do a deal with Reform to secure power.

Government ministers want to use former military bases as part of efforts close all asylum hotels.

Insisting that the MoD Bicester accommodation will be safe, the prime minister's deputy spokeswoman said such sites are "designed to be self-contained with 24/7 security and CCTV to minimise the impact on the local community".

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has also previously said it should not just be the poorest communities receiving dispersed refugees and asylum seekers.

Liberal Democrat MP Calum Miller told the BBC he was "very disappointed" but not "surprised" by the government's decision to grant planning permission.

Miller, whose constituency of Bicester and Woodstock includes the military site, said "the government was marking the government's application".

He said the decision "lays bare the weakness of the application and the many, many problems with it, because this is not a suitable site and it is not the right place to put a large-scale asylum centre".

articles.title: Iran targets US military site in Gulf for first time in two months as hopes for a deal fade
articles.summary: Iran said it targeted a US military installation in Bahrain early Friday in retaliation for what it described as an American attack on Iranian territory, marking its first attempt to strike a military facility in a Gulf state in more than two months.
articles.body: Iran said it targeted a US military installation in Bahrain early Friday in retaliation for what it described as an American attack on Iranian territory, marking its first attempt to strike a military facility in a Gulf state in more than two months. US Central Command (CENTCOM) said later Friday that American forces shot down two Iranian drones launched toward Bahrain, reporting no injuries or damage. “A few hours ago, the IRGC’s aerospace forces, in response to the enemy’s aerial aggression against a communication tower in Sirik, targeted and destroyed the early warning radar of the aggressor US military in Bahrain,” Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said, according to the semi-official Tasnim news agency, adding that “this is a serious warning” to Washington. CENTCOM said the claim that Iran attacked a radar system was false. While the US has continued striking Iranian targets around the Strait of Hormuz in recent weeks, Tehran has largely refrained from attacking American military installations in Gulf states since early September, focusing instead on disrupting shipping through the waterway. Meanwhile, Israel’s spy chief Roman Gofman was in Washington, DC, Friday, on a visit that comes as Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has recently sought to push the Trump administration into a return to war with Iran. Gofman expected to meet with CIA Director John Ratcliffe, a source familiar with the matter told CNN. His visit was first reported by Axios. CNN has reached out to the Israeli embassy in Washington, the White House and CIA for comment. ‘We don’t need a deal’ The Iranian attack came a day after US President Donald Trump said the US no longer needs a deal with Tehran and ordered his vice president to turn his focus elsewhere. “We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed!” Trump posted on Truth Social. “We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!” Trump also directed Vice President JD Vance, who had been tasked with leading negotiations between the US and Iran, “to focus his complete and total attention” on rooting out corruption and crime in Democratic states and cities. So far, Trump has held off on a renewed offensive and claimed his economic pressure campaign has been sufficient in weakening Tehran. Netanyahu had been pushing the US to carry out new strikes on Iran ahead of the US midterms. Iran has warned that it will not accept a stalemate as it comes under intense economic pressure from punishing US sanctions and a naval blockade. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said on Monday that Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei had instructed his government “to end the state of neither war nor peace,” telling him to “finish” the war with the US. He said the Islamic Republic “can negotiate with dignity, and can finish it (the war) with dignity.” The exchange comes as attacks on shipping in the strategic Strait of Hormuz reach a record high. October recorded 37 vessel attacks, Lloyd’s List reported Friday, the highest monthly total of the conflict. At least 14 more were confirmed in November, the maritime intelligence group said. Despite the attacks, oil has continued to flow through the waterway, with Middle East exports recovering faster than global oil demand. The International Energy Agency said Friday that the oil market is “showing tentative signs of rebalancing,” and that global oil supplies are surpassing demand for the first time since the outbreak of the Iran war. Iran has warned that any new escalation in the war would prompt it to dramatically expand its attacks, potentially targeting US interests as far away as Europe.

articles.title: A father left a 300-acre Minnesota farm to his son in a 1982 will, but a later will named his wife as owner; the appeals court ruled that an earlier ownership decree cannot be reopened
articles.summary: A Minnesota appeals court reversed a ruling reopening a dispute over a farm of about 300 acres in Red Lake County.
articles.body: A Minnesota appeals court reversed a ruling reopening a dispute over a farm of about 300 acres in Red Lake County. Clarence Vatthauer’s son, David, obtained a 2017 decree recognising his interest under his father’s 1982 will. Years later, Clarence’s daughter, Julie Ford, found a 1989 will leaving the farmland to his wife, Fern. According to a Minnesota Court of Appeals opinion filed on September 8, 2026, the decree could not be cancelled as void for lack of jurisdiction.The court said the district court erred by issuing it without the required medical-assistance-claim clearance, but the mistake did not remove its authority. It reversed the decision to vacate the decree and ordered recognition of its finality because no appeal was filed against it.How 300-acre farm becomes the centre of a dispute between siblingsClarence owned and farmed the Home Parcel, about 300 acres of farmland and cattle pasture in Red Lake County. His 1982 will gave Fern a life estate in the property, with the remainder passing to David. Clarence and Fern made new wills in 1989. Clarence’s later will revoked all earlier wills and left the Home Parcel to Fern in fee simple.Fern’s will left all her property to her children in equal shares. Clarence died in 2005. In 2015, David asked the district court to issue a decree of descent and submitted the 1982 will for probate. The court issued the decree in 2017, declaring David the fee owner of the Home Parcel.Missing medical-assistance clearance became central to the estate disputeThe 2017 decree was issued without a clearance for medical-assistance claims against Clarence’s estate. According to the law, “the court shall not enter a decree of descent until the petitioner has filed a clearance for medical assistance claims . . ., and until any medical assistance claims . . . have been paid, settled, or otherwise finally disposed of.”No one apparently raised the missing clearance when David sought the decree, and the record did not suggest that any family member knew about Clarence’s 1989 will. Fern’s health later declined. In 2022, Julie was appointed her guardian and contacted the law firm that had handled her parents’ estate planning. She then learned that both parents had made wills in 1989.Daughter challenges earlier decree after discovering father’s later willAfter discovering the later wills, Julie asked the district court to cancel the 2017 decree and probate Clarence’s 1989 will. She argued that the missing medical-assistance clearance meant the court had lacked subject-matter jurisdiction, making the decree void. She also sought relief under a court rule covering other reasons that might justify reopening a final order.Julie filed a separate action against David, claiming Fern owned the Home Parcel outright. Fern died in October 2023, and Julie sought probate of her 1989 will. The district court ordered both 1989 wills probated and cancelled the earlier decree, accepting Julie’s jurisdiction argument. It later ordered formal probate of Clarence’s 1989 will.Appeals court reverses decision to vacate 2017 decreeThe appeals court said the district court had jurisdiction over estate matters and that the relevant statutes did not clearly remove that authority when a medical-assistance clearance was missing. The failure to meet the statutory requirement was a judicial error, not a jurisdictional defect. The court said the error could have been challenged through an appeal within the 60-day period, but that period had expired years before the decree was vacated.It also rejected sending the case back to consider Julie’s alternative argument under the catchall court rule, because that rule cannot be used to correct judicial errors. The court reversed and remanded, directing the district court to recognise the 2017 decree as final.Disclaimer: This article is based on publicly available court records published by the Minnesota Court of Appeals. articles.title: 'You've been a victim': Woman Uber driver breaks down in tears after unknowingly delivering drugs to a Sydney resident
articles.summary: An unsuspecting Uber driver broke down in tears after discovering she had unknowingly delivered a package containing marijuana and cigarettes to the wrong
articles.body: An unsuspecting Uber driver broke down in tears after discovering she had unknowingly delivered a package containing marijuana and cigarettes to the wrong address in Sydney, Australia. The 24-year-old woman was caught up in an apparent drug delivery scheme after taking a parcel to a home in Rydalmere, in western Sydney. The package, which was intended for someone who did not live at the address, contained marijuana, Double Happiness cigarettes and noodles.The incident came to light after resident Adriano Valentino received a security camera alert showing a woman, an Uber driver, entering his family's garden. Alarmed by the unexpected visitor, he rushed home to investigate.His mother, who was inside the house, opened the package and was shocked by its contents.Valentino told news.com.au that he initially feared someone had entered the property to steal something. However, there had been no knock on the door before the parcel was left in the garden. Determined to find out who had delivered it, Valentino tracked down the Uber driver at a nearby Bunnings car park and confronted her. He also recorded their interaction.In the video, the visibly distressed driver insisted that she had no idea what was inside the package and had not checked the customer's bag."For privacy issues, we don't check the bags," she explained. "I'm sorry, I don't check bags ... I didn't know," she added.A check of the driver's Uber app reportedly showed that the parcel had been booked by a user named Adam and was meant for a recipient named Lisa. Neither person lived at the property where it was delivered. The woman insisted that she did not know that the packet contained marijuana. She also added that she did not deliver it to the wrong address; otherwise, she would have got an alert. But the person who booked the Uber delivery could not be reached when the woman tried.Police reassure driver she was a victimNSW Police confirmed that officers had spoken to the 24-year-old woman following reports of suspicious activity.The driver became increasingly distressed when police arrived, breaking down in tears as she repeatedly explained that drivers did not check the contents of customers' bags.An officer attempted to calm her down, telling her: "We believe everything you said, you've been a victim today."Valentino also defended the driver, directing his anger at the people who had allegedly used the delivery service to transport drugs. "F***king pathetic, you're terrorising a young lady using your Uber delivery service for your drugs," he said in the footage. "You got an innocent girl caught up in this; you guys are pathetic," he added.Speaking to news.com.au, Valentino said drivers should not be exploited in this manner. articles.title: Charity-run kitchens in Havana feed a growing number of Cubans as crisis deepens
articles.summary: As the state struggles to provide subsidized food, charity-run kitchens and food pantries have become a lifeline for vulnerable Cubans, including retired doctors and teachers.
articles.body: HAVANA — Every night, hundreds of people line up outside a charity-run food pantry in the heart of Havana, some sleeping on the sidewalk as they wait for what may be their only meal of the day. When the doors open at 7 a.m., people hurry inside carrying numbered plastic containers. With so many mouths to feed, volunteers follow a carefully organized routine: They wash the containers, call out the numbers and hand out portions of food. “We’re having a really rough time,” said Fernando Fernández, a 71-year-old retiree who regularly visits the Asociación Quisicuaba, a group that runs a community kitchen in Havana. “I have to arrive in the early morning. Sometimes I even have to get in line the day before.” Fernández, a former cook and security guard, is among a growing number of Cubans struggling to feed themselves as the country’s prolonged economic crisis deepens, worsened by U.S. energy restrictions, inflation and dwindling government resources. As the state struggles to provide subsidized food, charity-run kitchens and food pantries have become a lifeline for vulnerable Cubans, including retired doctors, teachers and former government workers. Supported by religious groups, international aid organizations and the United Nations, they provide what for many is their only reliable hot meal. Centers such as Quisicuaba, often housed in religious buildings or affiliated with faith-based groups, have proliferated across the island in recent years. Fernández, a former caretaker, once visited the soup kitchen with his 80-year-old wife, Josefa, but now goes alone because she is ill. The couple survives on her monthly pension of 3,200 Cuban pesos, a little more than $3, and assistance from Quisicuaba. On a recent morning, Marelys Ponce, a 34-year-old single mother, joined the line with two of her children. Her other three attend school, where they typically receive lunch. “I started coming here a little over a month ago because the situation is bad, and I don’t have the means to feed them,” she said, gesturing toward her children. “At least with this, they get something to eat.” Alongside Ponce and Fernández were men and women from a wide range of professions. Few were homeless. Most had long work histories or were still employed, but told the AP that their earnings were no longer enough to live on. ‘A new dimension of vulnerability’ Inside a vast kitchen equipped with more than 20 giant cauldrons, volunteers at Quisicuaba prepare a mixture of rice, eggs and pasta, sometimes with a little chicken, and pour chocolate milk into bottles. At 7 a.m., the doors open and distribution begins. The religious organization, supported by United Nations agencies and European aid groups, has identified about 12,500 vulnerable people in Havana. “You only need to walk through the streets of Havana and Cuba to see a new dimension of vulnerability,” Enrique Alemán, a physician and president of Quisicuaba, told The Associated Press. For decades, Cuba’s socialist system provided free education, healthcare and subsidized food, with most people employed by the state. Living standards were often modest, but basic needs — including food — were largely met. “We don’t see illiterate people here or other forms of marginalization, but people who are products of Cuban society facing particularly vulnerable circumstances,” Alemán said, pointing to growing financial, food and healthcare insecurity among families. The U.S. energy squeeze has severely disrupted life on the island, while tourism, once a major source of revenue, has declined sharply. Meanwhile, private businesses have expanded, widening the divide between entrepreneurs, higher-paid workers and Cubans receiving money from abroad, and state employees, retirees and others struggling to make ends meet. Private markets now offer imported goods that were scarce just a few years ago, but prices are beyond the reach of many Cubans. A carton of eggs costs 3,200 Cuban pesos, roughly a retiree’s monthly pension, while a bottle of cooking oil costs 2,700 pesos, or a bit less than $3. A doctor’s monthly salary can reach 15,000 pesos, equivalent to about $18. Inflation, which reached 28% in September from a year earlier, has further eroded purchasing power. Luis Carlos Battista, a Cuban American lawyer and analyst based in Spain, said growing poverty stems from domestic and external factors, including rising global food prices, the collapse of tourism during the COVID-19 pandemic and the impact of U.S. energy restrictions on food production. Cuba previously spent about $2 billion annually on food imports to support its rationing system, which provided households with staples including rice, beans, powdered milk, chicken, cooking oil and eggs. But authorities acknowledge that the economic crisis has left the government unable to maintain those imports, resulting in delayed or missing subsidized food rations. “While official rhetoric speaks of advancing toward socialism, a growing part of daily life operates under an increasingly individual logic,” researcher Lisbeth Moya González wrote in a recent essay published by La Joven Cuba, a prominent critical online platform. She said families increasingly must rely on private markets, remittances or community support to obtain what the state once guaranteed for all.
